clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 58-year-old male admitted to the emergency department with substernal chest pressure radiating to the left jaw for 45 minutes.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Diaphoretic, anxious, pale skin, S4 heart sound auscultated, lungs clear bilaterally.

diagnostic_results.12-lead ECG: ST-segment elevation in leads V1 through V4

provider_orders: Prepare for emergent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)

questions.stem: The client reports that the chest pressure has decreased from 8/10 to 5/10 after the first nitroglycerin dose. The blood pressure is now 104/66 mmHg, compared with 154/92 mmHg before the dose. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Withhold another nitroglycerin dose, reassess perfusion and symptoms, and promptly report the marked blood-pressure decrease
Repeat nitroglycerin because persistent chest pressure indicates that the first dose was ineffective
Administer the prescribed oral beta blocker now to reduce myocardial oxygen demand
Lower the head of the bed and elevate the legs to restore preload before reassessing

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: The substantial pressure decrease makes another vasodilator dose unsafe until hemodynamic status is reassessed; ongoing ischemia also requires urgent escalation.
rationales.B: Persistent pain alone does not justify repeating nitroglycerin when blood pressure has fallen substantially.
rationales.C: A beta blocker should not be given reflexively during evolving hemodynamic compromise; reassess and follow the acute coronary plan.
rationales.D: Routine leg elevation does not treat the cause and may worsen pulmonary congestion if ventricular function is impaired.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 72-year-old female with chronic systolic heart failure (LVEF 30%) being discharged home after acute decompensation.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Bibasilar lung fields clear, trace ankle edema, alert and oriented.
provider_orders: Discharge home with heart failure self-management teaching

questions.stem: The client is preparing for discharge after treatment for decompensated heart failure. Which statements show that the client can recognize early fluid retention and use the medication plan safely? Select all that apply.

options.text: I will weigh under the same conditions each morning and record the result.
I will contact the heart-failure team for the weight increase threshold in my written action plan, even if I feel well.
I can replace table salt with a potassium-based salt substitute because it contains no sodium.
I will take the loop diuretic early in the day unless my prescriber gives different instructions.
If I become dizzy after a dose, I will stop all my heart medicines until the next appointment.

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Standardized daily weights make trends more reliable and can reveal fluid retention before symptoms develop.
rationales.B: The client's individualized action-plan threshold should trigger contact; waiting for dyspnea can delay treatment.
rationales.C: Potassium-containing salt substitutes may cause hyperkalemia, particularly with renin-angiotensin system medicines or impaired renal function.
rationales.D: Morning dosing generally reduces nocturia; timing should still follow the prescribed regimen.
rationales.E: The client should report dizziness and obtain instructions rather than independently stopping multiple cardiac medicines.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 66-year-old male on telemetry post-coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) day 2.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Suddenly becomes lightheaded and diaphoretic; palpable radial pulse is weak and rapid.

diagnostic_results.Telemetry: Wide-complex regular tachycardia with a palpable pulse (monomorphic ventricular tachycardia)

questions.stem: The telemetry alarm shows a regular wide-complex rhythm at 176/min. The client is pale and diaphoretic, reports near-syncope, and has a blood pressure of 78/46 mmHg. A pulse is present. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate without delay?

options.text: Synchronized cardioversion while maintaining airway support and continuous monitoring
Unsynchronized defibrillation because any wide-complex tachycardia is a shockable rhythm
Adenosine administration before determining whether the rhythm is ventricular in origin
A vagal maneuver followed by reassessment of blood pressure

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: A pulse with hypotension and signs of poor perfusion indicates unstable tachycardia; synchronized cardioversion is the immediate treatment for unstable monomorphic VT with a pulse.
rationales.B: Defibrillation is used for pulseless VT/VF or when synchronization is not possible in a critically unstable rhythm; this client has a pulse and a regular rhythm suitable for synchronization.
rationales.C: Adenosine is not the first-line response to unstable wide-complex tachycardia and must not delay cardioversion.
rationales.D: Vagal maneuvers are inappropriate for an unstable wide-complex rhythm and would delay definitive treatment.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 69-year-old male with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) of the bilateral lower extremities.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Diminished dorsalis pedis pulses (1+), hair loss on lower legs, thick toenails, pain in calves after walking one block.

questions.stem: The client reports that calf pain is worse when the legs are elevated and improves when sitting at the bedside with the feet dependent. Which teaching best addresses this pattern while protecting the ischemic feet?

options.text: Use a neutral or dependent position for comfort and inspect the feet daily for pressure injury
Elevate the legs above the heart several times daily to improve venous return
Apply a heating pad on low setting for 20 minutes when the feet feel cold
Wear compression stockings during waking hours to reduce dependent edema

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Dependent positioning may improve arterial perfusion and relieve ischemic rest discomfort; daily inspection is important because impaired perfusion delays healing.
rationales.B: Elevation can further reduce arterial inflow and worsen ischemic pain in significant PAD.
rationales.C: Direct heat can cause burns, especially when sensation and perfusion are impaired.
rationales.D: Compression may compromise arterial inflow and should not be used without a specific vascular assessment and prescription.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 52-year-old female receiving a continuous unfractionated heparin infusion for an acute proximal left femoral deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Left calf warm and swollen; no active bleeding noted.

diagnostic_results.Venous Doppler: Occlusive thrombus in left superficial femoral vein

medications: Heparin sodium 25,000 units in 250 mL D5W infusing at 1,300 units/hr

questions.stem: The client's aPTT is 118 seconds against the facility's therapeutic range of 60–80 seconds. The client has new gingival oozing but is hemodynamically stable. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Stop or hold the infusion and follow the heparin nomogram, including repeat coagulation testing and bleeding assessment
Administer protamine immediately before determining the extent or severity of bleeding
Decrease the infusion slightly and repeat the aPTT with the next routine morning laboratory draw
Continue the infusion because aPTT values are expected to fluctuate during initial treatment

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: The supratherapeutic aPTT with active minor bleeding requires prompt protocol-based interruption or adjustment, focused assessment, and timely repeat testing.
rationales.B: Protamine is generally reserved for serious bleeding or urgent reversal; the nomogram and clinical severity guide its use.
rationales.C: A slight empiric reduction and delayed testing may leave the client anticoagulated above target.
rationales.D: Continuing unchanged despite an above-range result and bleeding increases hemorrhage risk.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 49-year-old male admitted to the ICU step-down unit with hypertensive emergency and acute kidney injury.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports throbbing occipital headache and blurred vision; no focal motor deficits.
medications: Nicardipine continuous IV infusion initiated at 5 mg/hr
provider_orders: Titrate nicardipine to reduce MAP by no more than 20-25% in the first hour

questions.stem: A client with a hypertensive emergency is receiving titrated IV nicardipine. The initial MAP is 150 mmHg. Which target best reflects safe early blood-pressure reduction when no condition-specific exception is present?

options.text: Reduce MAP by no more than approximately 20%–25% during the first hour, then titrate according to response
Normalize the blood pressure to below 120/80 mmHg within 15 minutes to prevent further organ injury
Maintain the initial MAP until all symptoms resolve, then lower it rapidly over the next hour
Reduce systolic pressure by at least 50% during the first hour regardless of neurologic status

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: In many hypertensive emergencies, controlled initial reduction limits ongoing injury while preserving perfusion to organs adapted to high pressure; targets vary by condition.
rationales.B: Abrupt normalization can cause cerebral, coronary, and renal hypoperfusion.
rationales.C: Leaving pressure untreated may worsen acute target-organ injury; reduction should be controlled, not deferred until symptoms resolve.
rationales.D: A fixed 50% reduction is excessive and ignores the affected organ and clinical context.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 36-year-old male admitted with fever, night sweats, and a new regurgitant mitral murmur.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Painful erythematous nodules on finger pads (Osler nodes) and splinter hemorrhages under fingernails.

diagnostic_results.Transthoracic Echocardiogram: Mobile vegetation on anterior mitral valve leaflet

medications: Vancomycin 1 g IV every 12 hours (pending blood cultures)
provider_orders: Obtain 3 sets of blood cultures from separate venipuncture sites before starting IV antibiotics

questions.stem: A client with suspected infective endocarditis is stable, and the first IV antibiotic dose has not yet been administered. Which actions belong in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Obtain the ordered blood-culture sets from separate venipuncture sites before antibiotics, if this does not delay emergency treatment
Assess for new focal neurologic deficits, acute limb pain, or flank pain that may indicate embolization
Monitor for heart-failure findings and changes in the character of the murmur
Stop antimicrobial therapy once the temperature has remained normal for 24 hours
Teach that prophylaxis is recommended before every dental cleaning for all clients with a history of any heart murmur

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Cultures obtained before antibiotics improve organism identification and guide targeted therapy when the client is stable enough for collection.
rationales.B: Vegetations can embolize to the brain, kidneys, spleen, or extremities; new symptoms require urgent evaluation.
rationales.C: Valve destruction and regurgitation can precipitate heart failure, so cardiopulmonary trends matter.
rationales.D: Endocarditis requires a prescribed full course; defervescence alone is not a stopping criterion.
rationales.E: Dental prophylaxis is limited to defined high-risk cardiac conditions and procedures, not every murmur.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 61-year-old female 6 hours post-percutaneous mitral valve repair.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Restless, cool extremities, jugular venous distension to the angle of the jaw, muffled heart sounds.

diagnostic_results.Bedside Ultrasound: Large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse

medications: 0.9% Sodium Chloride IV bolus 500 mL running
provider_orders: STAT cardiology consult for emergent pericardiocentesis

questions.stem: Six hours after a transcatheter mitral-valve procedure, the client becomes increasingly dyspneic. Blood pressure is falling, neck veins are distended, and heart sounds are difficult to hear. Which interpretation best links these findings?

options.text: Pericardial fluid is impairing diastolic filling and reducing cardiac output
Acute left ventricular failure is causing isolated pulmonary venous congestion
Aortic dissection is producing a widened pulse pressure and bounding peripheral pulses
Pulmonary embolism is causing increased left ventricular preload and a new diastolic murmur

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Hypotension, jugular venous distention, and muffled heart sounds after an invasive cardiac procedure strongly suggest tamponade with impaired ventricular filling.
rationales.B: Left-sided failure can cause crackles and pulmonary edema but does not best explain the combination of distended neck veins and muffled sounds in this setting.
rationales.C: The described hemodynamic pattern is not characteristic of aortic dissection; urgent evaluation for tamponade is needed.
rationales.D: Pulmonary embolism can cause acute right-heart strain, but it does not explain the classic tamponade pattern.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 74-year-old female with persistent atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc score 4) starting oral anticoagulation.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Irregularly irregular apical pulse at 78 bpm, no peripheral edema.

diagnostic_results.ECG: Atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response

questions.stem: A client taking warfarin asks whether leafy vegetables must be eliminated after an INR becomes therapeutic. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Keep vitamin K intake reasonably consistent and report major dietary changes so the anticoagulation plan can be adjusted
Avoid all foods containing vitamin K because even small amounts will reverse the anticoagulant effect
Eat extra spinach whenever bruising occurs to reduce the risk of bleeding
Change the amount of leafy vegetables from day to day because warfarin dosing is adjusted to each meal

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Consistency in vitamin K intake supports stable anticoagulation; large changes should be discussed with the anticoagulation team.
rationales.B: Eliminating vitamin K is unnecessary and can destabilize dietary intake and INR control.
rationales.C: Bruising requires assessment and possible INR review, not self-treatment with vitamin K-rich foods.
rationales.D: Day-to-day variation can contribute to INR instability.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 78-year-old male 12 hours after permanent dual-chamber pacemaker insertion via the left subclavian vein.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Dressing over left infraclavicular incision is dry and intact; client reports mild incisional soreness (3/10).

diagnostic_results.Chest X-ray: Atrial and ventricular leads properly positioned; no pneumothorax

medications: Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours PRN pain
Cefazolin 1 g IV every 8 hours x 2 doses
provider_orders: Immobilize left shoulder with sling for 24 hours

questions.stem: The client is 12 hours post-pacemaker insertion. Which discharge instruction best balances protection of the new lead with prevention of unnecessary long-term shoulder immobility?

options.text: Follow the implanting team's temporary lifting and shoulder-motion limits, and report syncope, persistent hiccups, or new diaphragmatic twitching
Keep the ipsilateral arm immobilized in a sling continuously for 6 weeks, including during hygiene
Begin repeated overhead stretching tomorrow to prevent adhesive capsulitis
Avoid all household appliances that generate electromagnetic fields, including microwave ovens

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Temporary movement restrictions vary by device and clinician; new presyncope or unusual stimulation symptoms may indicate lead or device problems.
rationales.B: Prolonged complete immobilization is not routinely required and can cause stiffness; follow the specific postimplant plan.
rationales.C: Early unrestricted overhead movement may stress the lead; exercises should follow the implant team's timing.
rationales.D: Modern household appliances such as microwave ovens are generally safe when functioning properly; broad avoidance is unnecessary.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 71-year-old male admitted for observation of a known 5.8 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) awaiting endovascular repair.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Suddenly reports severe, tearing lower back and flank pain; skin is pale, cool, and clammy.

questions.stem: While awaiting repair of a known abdominal aortic aneurysm, the client develops abrupt severe back pain, pallor, diaphoresis, and a falling blood pressure. Which response is the priority?

options.text: Activate the emergency vascular response, maintain large-bore IV access, and prepare for immediate definitive evaluation and repair
Palpate the abdomen repeatedly to determine whether the aneurysm has enlarged
Administer the scheduled antihypertensive and reassess the pain after its peak effect
Rapidly infuse enough crystalloid to restore the blood pressure to the client's usual baseline

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: The presentation is concerning for rupture; rapid escalation, access, blood-product readiness, and definitive vascular management are priorities.
rationales.B: Deep or repeated palpation can be harmful and does not establish rupture.
rationales.C: A routine oral medication delays emergency management and may worsen hypotension.
rationales.D: Uncontrolled crystalloid loading to a normal baseline can worsen bleeding; resuscitation targets are directed by the emergency team.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 64-year-old male in the CCU 18 hours after an extensive anterior wall myocardial infarction.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Lethargic, cool mottled extremities, bilateral crackles halfway up lung fields, JVD present, urine output 12 mL over the past hour.
provider_orders: Titrate vasoactive drips per CCU protocol

questions.stem: Complete the bowtie using the client's post-MI findings: identify the most likely hemodynamic problem, select two immediate interventions, and select two measures that best show whether perfusion is improving.

actions: Initiate dobutamine and norepinephrine infusions as prescribed
Administer supplemental high-flow oxygen or prepare for noninvasive ventilation
Infuse 3,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride over 1 hour
Administer IV furosemide 80 mg push before stabilizing blood pressure
Place the client in Trendelenburg position
parameters: Hourly urine output and serum lactate levels
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) and lung sounds

actions: Initiate dobutamine and norepinephrine infusions as prescribed
Administer supplemental high-flow oxygen or prepare for noninvasive ventilation
parameters: Hourly urine output and serum lactate levels
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) and lung sounds

rationales.condition: Severe LV dysfunction after MI, hypotension, elevated lactate, oliguria, JVD, and crackles indicate cardiogenic rather than hypovolemic or distributive shock.
rationales.actions: Prescribed inotropic and vasopressor support can improve contractility and perfusion pressure; oxygenation support addresses hypoxemia. A large unassessed crystalloid bolus can worsen pulmonary edema.
rationales.parameters: Urine output and lactate trend reflect end-organ perfusion; MAP and lung findings help evaluate perfusion pressure and pulmonary congestion.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 81-year-old female taking digoxin and furosemide for heart failure and atrial fibrillation.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports nausea, anorexia, and yellow-green halos around ceiling lights.

diagnostic_results.ECG: Sinus bradycardia with frequent premature ventricular contractions (PVCs)

provider_orders: Draw STAT electrolytes and digoxin level

questions.stem: The client taking digoxin and furosemide reports nausea and yellow-green halos. The ECG shows frequent ventricular ectopy, and potassium is 2.8 mEq/L. Which factor most likely increased myocardial sensitivity to digoxin?

options.text: Reduced extracellular potassium increases digoxin binding at the sodium-potassium ATPase
Low potassium increases renal clearance of digoxin and causes rebound toxicity
Hypokalemia blocks digoxin absorption, causing accumulation of an active metabolite
Low potassium directly increases serum calcium and produces the visual disturbance

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Potassium competes with digoxin at the sodium-potassium ATPase; hypokalemia increases binding and toxicity risk.
rationales.B: Hypokalemia does not increase digoxin clearance; renal function and drug interactions influence serum exposure.
rationales.C: The mechanism is not impaired absorption or metabolite accumulation.
rationales.D: The visual symptoms and dysrhythmias are consistent with digoxin toxicity; this option gives an incorrect electrolyte mechanism.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 57-year-old male returned to the step-down unit 30 minutes ago following right femoral artery coronary angiography with stent placement.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Nurse enters the room for routine post-procedure checks and observes bright red blood pooling beneath the client's right groin dressing.

diagnostic_results.Procedure note: 6-French right femoral arterial sheath removed with manual compression

medications: Clopidogrel 600 mg loading dose given in cath lab
provider_orders: Bed rest with right leg straight for 6 hours

questions.stem: Thirty minutes after femoral coronary angiography, the nurse finds active bright-red bleeding beneath the groin dressing. Place the actions in the safest sequence, maintaining pressure while assistance is obtained.

items: Don sterile gloves and apply firm manual pressure 1 to 2 cm above the percutaneous puncture site
Activate the call light to summon assistance and have another nurse notify the interventional cardiologist
Assess vital signs and right dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial pulses while maintaining continuous pressure
Apply a sterile pressure dressing once hemostasis is achieved and document blood loss and neurovascular status

correct_response: Don sterile gloves and apply firm manual pressure 1 to 2 cm above the percutaneous puncture site
Activate the call light to summon assistance and have another nurse notify the interventional cardiologist
Assess vital signs and right dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial pulses while maintaining continuous pressure
Apply a sterile pressure dressing once hemostasis is achieved and document blood loss and neurovascular status

rationales.1: Immediate firm pressure proximal to the skin entry point compresses the arterial puncture and limits blood loss.
rationales.2: Summon help and notify the procedural team while maintaining continuous pressure at the bedside.
rationales.3: Assess hemodynamic stability and distal perfusion without interrupting hemostasis.
rationales.4: After bleeding is controlled, apply the prescribed dressing and document the event and neurovascular findings.
rationales.summary: Active arterial bleeding requires immediate sustained direct pressure; additional assessment and escalation occur without releasing pressure.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 63-year-old female 1 day post-total hip arthroplasty.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Alert, surgical hip dressing dry, mild bilateral lower extremity trace edema.
provider_orders: Sequential compression devices (SCDs) while in bed

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing a prefilled enoxaparin syringe for a client after hip arthroplasty. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Inject into the anterolateral or posterolateral abdominal tissue, leave the air bubble in the prefilled syringe, and do not massage afterward
Inject into the deltoid muscle and aspirate before depressing the plunger
Expel the air bubble, inject into the abdomen, then massage firmly to distribute the medication
Inject into the thigh through clothing and apply pressure for 5 minutes

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Subcutaneous abdominal administration is standard; the air bubble in many prefilled syringes helps deliver the full dose, and massage increases bruising.
rationales.B: Enoxaparin is not administered intramuscularly; aspiration is not recommended for routine subcutaneous injection.
rationales.C: Expelling the bubble and massaging may increase bruising or reduce accurate delivery.
rationales.D: Injection through clothing is not appropriate technique; the site should be prepared and exposed.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 34-year-old male admitted with sharp, pleuritic substernal chest pain following a viral upper respiratory infection.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Pain worsens when lying flat and improves when sitting upright and leaning forward; high-pitched scratchy sound heard at left sternal border.

diagnostic_results.12-lead ECG: Diffuse concave upward ST-segment elevation across most leads with PR-segment depression

medications: Ibuprofen 600 mg PO every 8 hours with food
provider_orders: Echocardiogram to evaluate for pericardial effusion

questions.stem: A client with acute pericarditis develops increasing dyspnea, narrowing pulse pressure, jugular venous distention, and a new decrease in blood pressure. Which complication should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Pericardial effusion progressing to cardiac tamponade
Papillary muscle rupture causing acute mitral regurgitation
Aortic stenosis causing fixed left ventricular outflow obstruction
Uncomplicated pleurisy causing pain-limited inspiration

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: The evolving signs suggest impaired cardiac filling from an enlarging effusion and require immediate escalation.
rationales.B: Papillary muscle rupture usually causes acute pulmonary edema and a new murmur after myocardial infarction.
rationales.C: Aortic stenosis is not an acute complication of pericarditis and does not explain this progression.
rationales.D: Pleurisy can cause pain and shallow breathing but not the hemodynamic pattern described.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 68-year-old male admitted with an acute exacerbation of severe COPD.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Using accessory neck muscles, prolonged expiratory phase with diffuse expiratory wheezes, barrel chest.

laboratory_results.ABG: pH 7.31, PaCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 29 mEq/L, PaO2 52 mmHg

diagnostic_results.Chest X-ray: Hyperinflated lung fields, flattened diaphragms, no focal infiltrate

provider_orders: Titrate supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 88% to 92%

questions.stem: The client with an acute COPD exacerbation has an order to maintain SpO2 between 88% and 92%. The client is alert, breathing spontaneously, and requires a controlled oxygen concentration. Which device best supports precise titration?

options.text: Venturi mask at the prescribed FiO2, adjusted to maintain the target range
Non-rebreather mask at maximum flow until saturation reaches 100%
Simple face mask at 10 L/min without reassessment
Nasal cannula at 6 L/min because higher flow is needed for all exacerbations

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: A Venturi system delivers a controlled FiO2 and is useful when precise oxygen titration is needed.
rationales.B: Routine pursuit of 100% saturation can provide excessive oxygen and is not the prescribed target.
rationales.C: A simple mask does not provide the same precision and should be titrated to clinical response.
rationales.D: A fixed high nasal-cannula flow is not appropriate for every client and may exceed the ordered target.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 44-year-old male with a right-sided chest tube connected to a wet-suction water-seal drainage system for a spontaneous pneumothorax.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Mild incisional pain at insertion site, diminished right breath sounds at base, trachea midline.
medications: Morphine 2 mg IV every 3 hours PRN pain
provider_orders: Chest tube to -20 cm H2O suction
Keep sterile petroleum gauze and hemostats at bedside

questions.stem: The nurse assesses a client with a chest tube after treatment of a pneumothorax. Which findings require prompt intervention? Select all that apply.

options.text: Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber after checking that the system connections are secure
Tidaling in the water-seal chamber that varies with respiration
New bright-red drainage of 250 mL in one hour
The chest tube becomes disconnected from the drainage tubing
The collection unit remains upright and below the level of the chest

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Persistent bubbling in the water seal suggests an air leak; assess the client and system, then locate and correct the leak per policy.
rationales.B: Tidaling can be an expected reflection of pressure changes; its absence or presence must be interpreted with the clinical picture.
rationales.C: A sudden large volume of bright-red drainage may indicate hemorrhage and requires immediate assessment and escalation.
rationales.D: Disconnection breaks the closed system; restore the prescribed system promptly using facility protocol while assessing the client.
rationales.E: Keeping the unit upright and below chest level is correct practice.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 47-year-old female 3 days post-pelvic surgery who suddenly develops acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Tachypneic, anxious, clear lung sounds on auscultation, right calf swollen and tender.

diagnostic_results.CT Pulmonary Angiogram: Large bilateral saddle pulmonary emboli with right ventricular strain

questions.stem: Three days after pelvic surgery, the client suddenly becomes dyspneic and anxious. SpO2 is 84%, heart rate is 128/min, and blood pressure is 106/68 mmHg. Which action should the nurse take first while activating emergency assistance?

options.text: Support oxygenation, position to ease breathing, and rapidly assess airway and circulation
Administer the prescribed heparin bolus before confirming that the client can tolerate anticoagulation
Obtain a 12-lead ECG before intervening because pulmonary embolism is a diagnosis of exclusion
Insert a urinary catheter to quantify perfusion before providing oxygen

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Acute hypoxemia and respiratory distress require immediate support of oxygenation and ABC assessment while the emergency response is activated.
rationales.B: Anticoagulation may be indicated after rapid evaluation, but it does not replace immediate stabilization and requires attention to bleeding risk.
rationales.C: ECG may assist evaluation but must not delay treatment of severe hypoxemia.
rationales.D: Urine-output monitoring is not the first intervention in an acutely hypoxemic client.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 53-year-old male mechanically ventilated in the ICU for severe ARDS secondary to urosepsis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Sedated (RASS -3), coarse bilateral crackles throughout all lung fields.

laboratory_results.ABG: pH 7.29, PaCO2 50 mmHg, PaO2 54 mmHg (PaO2/FiO2 ratio = 67.5)

provider_orders: Low tidal volume lung-protective ventilation (6 mL/kg IBW)
Initiate prone positioning protocol for 16 hours/day

questions.stem: A client with severe ARDS remains hypoxemic despite lung-protective ventilation and appropriate PEEP. The team plans prolonged prone sessions. Which physiologic change most directly explains the expected improvement?

options.text: Improved recruitment of dependent dorsal lung regions and a more even distribution of ventilation relative to perfusion
A reduction in pulmonary capillary permeability that rapidly removes alveolar edema
An increase in tidal volume that stretches previously collapsed alveoli beyond their normal capacity
A decrease in pulmonary blood flow that reduces the amount of blood exposed to poorly ventilated alveoli

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Proning redistributes transpulmonary pressure and recruits dorsal lung units, improving ventilation-perfusion matching and oxygenation.
rationales.B: Prone positioning does not directly reverse the inflammatory capillary leak causing ARDS.
rationales.C: Lung-protective ventilation aims to avoid excessive tidal volume and overdistension.
rationales.D: The benefit is improved regional matching, not global reduction of pulmonary perfusion.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 27-year-old female with moderate persistent asthma attending an outpatient follow-up visit.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Lungs clear on auscultation, speaks in full sentences, using rescue inhaler 4 times per week.
medications: Fluticasone propionate HFA 2 puffs twice daily
Albuterol HFA 2 puffs every 4-6 hours PRN
provider_orders: Review inhaler technique and asthma action plan

questions.stem: The client uses inhaled fluticasone twice daily and reports a new white coating in the mouth with soreness. Which teaching best prevents recurrence while supporting continued controller therapy?

options.text: Rinse the mouth and gargle with water after each dose, then spit the water out; use a spacer if appropriate for the device
Stop fluticasone whenever symptoms improve and restart it during wheezing episodes
Swallow water immediately after inhalation so the medication reaches the stomach
Use albuterol immediately before every fluticasone dose to prevent oral candidiasis

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Rinsing and spitting reduces oropharyngeal steroid residue and candidiasis risk; a spacer can reduce deposition for compatible inhalers.
rationales.B: Inhaled corticosteroids are maintenance therapy and should not be stopped solely because symptoms improve unless the prescriber adjusts the plan.
rationales.C: Swallowing does not remove medication from the oral mucosa and is not the recommended prevention strategy.
rationales.D: A bronchodilator may be used before a controller when prescribed, but it does not prevent local candidiasis.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 62-year-old male 48 hours post-surgical tracheostomy placement for laryngeal carcinoma.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Suddenly begins coughing forcefully during repositioning, dislodging the entire tracheostomy tube onto his chest.

diagnostic_results.Airway note: Fresh tracheostomy tract (<72 hours old); stay sutures present

provider_orders: Keep spare tracheostomy tube (same size and one size smaller) and obturator at bedside

questions.stem: A tracheostomy placed 48 hours ago becomes completely dislodged. The client is coughing, anxious, and has falling oxygen saturation. What is the safest immediate nursing response?

options.text: Call for emergency airway assistance, provide oxygen to the face and stoma as appropriate, and prepare for expert airway management without blind reinsertion
Force the spare tube through the immature stoma using the obturator before calling for help
Seal the stoma with an occlusive dressing and provide oxygen only by nasal cannula
Wait for the surgeon at bedside because any attempt to oxygenate may close the stoma

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: A fresh tract can close or create a false passage; immediate oxygenation and expert airway support are essential, and reinsertion should follow the facility's emergency algorithm by trained personnel.
rationales.B: Blind forceful reinsertion in a fresh tract can create a false passage and worsen airway loss.
rationales.C: Occluding the stoma without knowing the airway anatomy can prevent ventilation; oxygen delivery must account for the upper airway and stoma.
rationales.D: Oxygenation and emergency assistance must begin immediately; waiting without intervention is unsafe.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 41-year-old male admitted with a 4-week history of productive cough, hemoptysis, fever, and 15-pound unintentional weight loss.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Cachectic, coarse crackles in right upper lobe.
provider_orders: Baseline liver function tests and visual acuity exam

questions.stem: A client is admitted with suspected infectious pulmonary tuberculosis. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the client in an airborne infection isolation room with the door closed
Wear a fit-tested N95 or higher-level respirator when entering the room
Place a surgical mask on the client during medically necessary transport and limit transport
Use a standard surgical mask instead of a respirator if the nurse remains more than 1 meter away
Coordinate sputum collection and treatment while maintaining airborne precautions

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Airborne isolation in an appropriate room is required for suspected infectious pulmonary TB.
rationales.B: A fit-tested respirator is required for staff entering the room.
rationales.C: Source control and limiting transport reduce transmission risk during necessary movement.
rationales.D: Distance alone does not replace respiratory protection for airborne precautions.
rationales.E: Diagnostic testing and treatment should proceed without relaxing isolation measures.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 66-year-old female mechanically ventilated via an endotracheal tube for pneumonia-induced respiratory failure.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Restless, biting on the oral endotracheal tube, coarse rhonchi present; high-pressure ventilator alarm sounds continuously.

diagnostic_results.Chest X-ray: ET tube tip 3.5 cm above carina; right lower lobe infiltrate

provider_orders: Volume-assist control ventilation, Vt 420 mL, PEEP 8 cm H2O

questions.stem: A ventilated client triggers a high-pressure alarm. The client is restless, oxygen saturation is falling, and coarse breath sounds are heard. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Assess the client and airway patency, then suction if secretions are present while another team member checks the circuit
Silence the alarm and increase the high-pressure limit to prevent repeated alerts
Disconnect the ventilator and leave the client unsupported while troubleshooting the machine
Decrease the prescribed PEEP and tidal volume before assessing the client

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: High-pressure alarms commonly reflect increased resistance or reduced compliance; assess the patient first and address secretions or obstruction while checking the circuit.
rationales.B: Changing alarm limits can conceal deterioration and does not correct the cause.
rationales.C: If disconnection is necessary, the client must be supported with an appropriate manual ventilation strategy; leaving the client unsupported is unsafe.
rationales.D: Ventilator settings should not be changed blindly before identifying the cause and assessing the client.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 84-year-old female brought from an assisted living facility with new-onset acute confusion and lethargy.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Disoriented to place and time (baseline alert and oriented x4), bronchial breath sounds and egophony in left lower lung field.
provider_orders: Incentive spirometry every hour while awake

questions.stem: An 84-year-old resident develops new confusion, reduced appetite, and a respiratory rate of 26/min. Temperature is 37.2°C, and the client has a new cough. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's next action?

options.text: Pneumonia remains possible despite the absence of a high fever; assess oxygenation and escalate the acute change
Pneumonia is unlikely because older adults consistently develop high fever with bacterial infection
Confusion is most likely chronic dementia and does not require an acute assessment
The findings indicate dehydration alone, so oral fluids should be offered before further assessment

rationales.summary: Use the complete clinical picture and the client's changing response to select the safest action; reassess and escalate when findings indicate deterioration.
rationales.A: Older adults may present with delirium, tachypnea, or functional decline rather than prominent fever; acute respiratory assessment is warranted.
rationales.B: Older adults may have blunted febrile responses, so absence of high fever does not exclude infection.
rationales.C: A sudden change in cognition must be evaluated for acute illness rather than attributed to baseline dementia.
rationales.D: Dehydration may coexist, but respiratory symptoms and tachypnea require assessment for infection and hypoxemia.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 59-year-old male undergoing bedside ultrasound-guided right thoracentesis for a large malignant pleural effusion.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Sitting upright leaning over an overbed table; 1,100 mL of serosanguinous fluid drained so far.
provider_orders: Limit fluid removal to <= 1,000-1,500 mL per session

questions.stem: During ultrasound-guided thoracentesis, the client develops persistent coughing, chest tightness, and a sudden drop in oxygen saturation from 96% to 88%. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the procedure, support oxygenation, and promptly assess for pneumothorax or re-expansion pulmonary edema
Encourage deeper breathing and continue drainage until the prescribed volume is removed
Place the client flat and ask the client to suppress coughing
Administer an oral antitussive and reassess oxygen saturation in 15 minutes

rationales.summary: The safest response is based on the change in the client's clinical condition and the risk of rapid deterioration.
rationales.A: New respiratory symptoms and desaturation during thoracentesis require stopping fluid removal and immediate assessment for complications.
rationales.B: Continuing drainage may worsen the complication and delay treatment.
rationales.C: Supine positioning may worsen breathing and suppressing cough does not address the cause.
rationales.D: An oral antitussive delays assessment and is inappropriate during acute respiratory deterioration.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 23-year-old male with cystic fibrosis admitted for an acute pulmonary exacerbation.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Digital clubbing, productive cough with thick tenacious green sputum, scattered rhonchi, BMI 18.2 kg/m2.

diagnostic_results.Chest CT: Bilateral upper-lobe bronchiectasis and mucus plugging

provider_orders: High-frequency chest wall oscillation vest twice daily

questions.stem: A client with cystic fibrosis is admitted with increased sputum, weight loss, and frequent bulky stools. Which interventions address the client's airway clearance and malabsorption? Select all that apply.

options.text: Administer a prescribed bronchodilator before airway-clearance therapy when indicated
Give pancreatic enzymes with meals and snacks according to the prescribed dose
Provide high-calorie, high-protein nutrition and prescribed fat-soluble vitamins
Schedule chest physiotherapy immediately after a full meal to improve tolerance
Assess weight trends, stool characteristics, and respiratory response to treatment

rationales.summary: The safest response is based on the change in the client's clinical condition and the risk of rapid deterioration.
rationales.A: Bronchodilation before airway clearance can improve airflow and secretion mobilization.
rationales.B: Pancreatic enzymes must be taken with food to aid digestion and absorption.
rationales.C: Increased energy needs and fat malabsorption often require calorie-dense nutrition and vitamins A, D, E, and K.
rationales.D: Airway clearance immediately after meals may provoke vomiting; schedule around meals according to tolerance.
rationales.E: Weight and stool trends help assess nutrition and enzyme effectiveness; respiratory reassessment evaluates treatment response.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 22-year-old female in the emergency department with severe asthma exacerbation refractory to three consecutive albuterol/ipratropium nebulizers.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Sitting upright unable to speak single words, markedly decreased breath sounds with absent wheezing ('silent chest'), diaphoretic.

questions.stem: A client in status asthmaticus initially had loud wheezing but now has minimal air movement, increasing fatigue, and PaCO2 rising from 28 to 52 mmHg. How should the nurse interpret this change?

options.text: Ventilatory failure is developing because airflow is critically limited and respiratory muscles are tiring
Bronchospasm is resolving because wheezing has diminished
The rising PaCO2 is an expected effect of inhaled beta-agonists and requires no escalation
The client is hyperventilating effectively and should be encouraged to breathe more slowly

rationales.summary: The safest response is based on the change in the client's clinical condition and the risk of rapid deterioration.
rationales.A: A quiet chest with rising CO2 and fatigue indicates poor ventilation and impending respiratory failure; prepare for urgent escalation and airway support.
rationales.B: Wheezing may disappear when airflow becomes critically low, not because obstruction has resolved.
rationales.C: Rising PaCO2 in severe asthma is a danger sign, not a benign medication effect.
rationales.D: The client is retaining CO2 because ventilation is failing, not hyperventilating effectively.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 54-year-old male admitted for laparoscopic cholecystectomy with a documented history of severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).
clinical_scenario.assessment: BMI 36 kg/m2, neck circumference 18 inches, uses CPAP at 12 cm H2O nightly at home.
medications: Hydromorphone 0.5 mg IV every 3 hours PRN severe pain
provider_orders: Use home CPAP machine during all sleep periods

questions.stem: A client with severe obstructive sleep apnea is recovering from abdominal surgery and has received IV opioids. The client is drowsy but arousable, with intermittent obstructive snoring and desaturation during sleep. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Position to maintain airway patency, resume prescribed CPAP when appropriate, and intensify respiratory monitoring
Administer a benzodiazepine to reduce anxiety and promote uninterrupted sleep
Withhold all analgesia and allow the client to sleep without monitoring
Place the client flat and discontinue CPAP because positive pressure can cause gastric distention

rationales.summary: The safest response is based on the change in the client's clinical condition and the risk of rapid deterioration.
rationales.A: OSA and opioids increase risk of obstruction and hypoventilation; airway positioning, prescribed CPAP, opioid-sparing analgesia, and monitoring are important.
rationales.B: Sedatives can worsen airway obstruction and respiratory depression.
rationales.C: Pain control remains necessary, but close monitoring and safer analgesic strategies are required.
rationales.D: Flat positioning can worsen obstruction, and CPAP should not be stopped without clinical reason.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 48-year-old female with a 25-pack-year smoking history starting transdermal nicotine patch therapy (21 mg/24 hr).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Motivated to quit smoking, mild morning smoker's cough, lungs clear.

questions.stem: A client using a nicotine patch asks whether the patch should remain on while sleeping and whether smoking is permitted during treatment. Which teaching is most accurate?

options.text: Follow the prescribed wear schedule, remove the old patch before applying a new one, rotate sites, and avoid smoking while using it unless specifically directed
Apply a second patch if cravings occur and leave both patches in place overnight
Cut the patch in half to adjust the dose and apply it over irritated skin
Place the new patch over the previous patch to maintain a steady nicotine level

rationales.summary: The safest response is based on the change in the client's clinical condition and the risk of rapid deterioration.
rationales.A: Correct patch use includes removing the old patch, rotating clean dry sites, and following product-specific wear instructions; concurrent smoking can increase nicotine toxicity risk.
rationales.B: Adding patches without direction can cause overdose.
rationales.C: Patches should not be cut unless the product is specifically designed for it; irritated skin should be avoided.
rationales.D: Leaving an old patch in place can cause excess nicotine exposure.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 65-year-old male brought to the emergency department 55 minutes after sudden onset of right-sided hemiplegia and expressive aphasia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score 14, alert, unable to lift right arm or leg.

diagnostic_results.Non-contrast Head CT: No intracranial hemorrhage or mass effect

provider_orders: Prepare for intravenous tenecteplase (TNK) thrombolytic therapy
Lower blood pressure to < 185/110 mmHg prior to thrombolysis

questions.stem: The client arrives with aphasia and right-sided weakness that began 70 minutes ago. Point-of-care glucose is 48 mg/dL. The stroke team is evaluating eligibility for thrombolysis. Which action should the nurse anticipate first?

options.text: Treat the hypoglycemia promptly and reassess the neurologic deficits before proceeding with thrombolysis decisions
Administer alteplase immediately because the symptom-onset window is more important than the glucose result
Give aspirin and clopidogrel before repeating the neurologic assessment
Lower the blood pressure rapidly to below 120/80 mmHg before obtaining brain imaging

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Hypoglycemia can mimic acute stroke and must be corrected promptly; persistent deficits then require continued stroke evaluation and imaging-based decisions.
rationales.B: Treatable mimics and contraindications must be assessed; thrombolysis should not be given before addressing severe hypoglycemia.
rationales.C: Antiplatelet therapy is not given before thrombolysis decisions and may increase bleeding risk if thrombolysis is used.
rationales.D: Rapid normalization of blood pressure is not routinely indicated and can reduce cerebral perfusion; imaging and protocol-specific thresholds guide management.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 39-year-old male in the neuro-ICU following a severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) with an intraventricular ICP monitor.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score 8 (E2 V2 M4), pupils 4 mm equal and sluggishly reactive.

diagnostic_results.ICP monitor: Sustained ICP 24 mmHg (normal 5-15 mmHg), CPP 80 mmHg

medications: Mannitol 0.5 g/kg IV PRN ICP > 20 mmHg

questions.stem: A client with traumatic brain injury has an ICP of 24 mmHg and worsening headache. Which interventions should the nurse implement while escalating the sustained elevation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maintain the head midline and elevate the head of bed about 30 degrees if not contraindicated
Avoid prolonged hip flexion and unnecessary stimulation that can increase intrathoracic or intracranial pressure
Coordinate care to allow rest periods and prevent repeated painful stimulation
Suction the endotracheal tube on a fixed schedule every hour even when secretions are absent
Place the client in Trendelenburg position to increase cerebral venous return

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Midline alignment and modest head elevation promote venous drainage when hemodynamically tolerated.
rationales.B: Hip flexion, straining, and avoidable stimulation can impede venous return or provoke ICP elevations.
rationales.C: Clustering care with rest periods reduces avoidable stimulation while the client is monitored closely.
rationales.D: Unnecessary suctioning can transiently raise ICP; suction only when clinically indicated and preoxygenate as appropriate.
rationales.E: Trendelenburg impairs cerebral venous drainage and may worsen ICP.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 31-year-old male with a C6 complete spinal cord injury admitted for urinary tract infection treatment.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Suddenly reports a pounding headache; profuse diaphoresis and flushing noted above the clavicles, goosebumps and pallor below.

diagnostic_results.Bladder scan: 580 mL urine; indwelling Foley tubing found kinked beneath leg

questions.stem: A client with a C6 spinal cord injury develops a pounding headache, flushing above the lesion, bradycardia, and BP 214/118 mmHg. The Foley tubing is kinked and the bladder scan shows 580 mL. Place the interventions in priority order.

items: Elevate the head of the bed to 90 degrees (high Fowler position) and lower the legs
Loosen any tight clothing, abdominal binder, or anti-embolism stockings
Uncoiling/unkinking the Foley catheter tubing to drain the distended urinary bladder
Recheck blood pressure every 2 to 5 minutes and administer prescribed antihypertensive therapy if BP remains elevated

correct_response: Elevate the head of the bed to 90 degrees (high Fowler position) and lower the legs
Loosen any tight clothing, abdominal binder, or anti-embolism stockings
Uncoiling/unkinking the Foley catheter tubing to drain the distended urinary bladder
Recheck blood pressure every 2 to 5 minutes and administer prescribed antihypertensive therapy if BP remains elevated

rationales.1: Sit the client upright with legs lowered to reduce blood pressure through orthostatic pooling while summoning assistance.
rationales.2: Remove external constriction that may be contributing to the noxious stimulus.
rationales.3: Bladder distention is a common trigger; correct the kink and allow drainage without forceful irrigation.
rationales.4: Frequent blood-pressure reassessment is essential; give prescribed rapid-acting antihypertensive if severe hypertension persists after trigger removal.
rationales.summary: Autonomic dysreflexia is a hypertensive emergency in a client with a lesion at or above T6. Reduce blood pressure promptly, remove constriction, and eliminate the triggering stimulus.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 29-year-old female with epilepsy admitted after breakthrough generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Client suddenly cries out, loses consciousness, and develops generalized tonic-clonic motor activity.
medications: Lorazepam 2 mg IV push PRN seizure > 5 minutes

questions.stem: A client begins a generalized tonic-clonic seizure while standing beside the bed. Which action should the nurse take during the seizure?

options.text: Guide the client to the floor, protect the head, loosen restrictive clothing, and turn to the side when feasible
Restrain the arms and legs to prevent musculoskeletal injury
Insert an oral airway between clenched teeth to prevent tongue injury
Leave the client briefly to obtain IV medication before protecting the airway

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Protecting from injury, supporting a side-lying position when possible, and timing the seizure are appropriate immediate actions.
rationales.B: Restraints can cause injury and do not stop seizure activity.
rationales.C: Nothing should be forced into the mouth during an active seizure; this can cause dental and airway injury.
rationales.D: Stay with the client, summon help, and protect the airway and environment; medication follows protocol and does not replace immediate safety.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 45-year-old female with generalized myasthenia gravis admitted with worsening dysphagia, diplopia, and generalized weakness.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Weak cough, nasal speech, shallow respirations, uses accessory muscles.

diagnostic_results.Bedside Spirometry: Forced vital capacity (FVC) 11 mL/kg (decreased from 28 mL/kg)

medications: Pyridostigmine 60 mg PO every 4 hours while awake
provider_orders: Measure FVC and negative inspiratory force (NIF) every 2 hours
Hold oral medications if dysphagia worsens

questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis develops a weak cough, difficulty handling secretions, and a forced vital capacity that has fallen from 24 to 14 mL/kg. Oxygen saturation remains 95% on room air. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Escalate immediately for critical-care airway assessment and prepare for ventilatory support
Administer the next oral pyridostigmine dose and reassess respiratory strength in 2 hours
Encourage repeated incentive spirometry and ambulation to improve respiratory muscle endurance
Provide oral fluids to thin secretions and reduce the work of coughing

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Declining vital capacity, weak cough, and secretion difficulty signal impending respiratory failure; oxygen saturation can remain normal until late.
rationales.B: Oral medication may be unsafe with bulbar weakness and must not delay airway support.
rationales.C: Exercise and incentive spirometry are not adequate treatment for rapidly worsening neuromuscular respiratory weakness.
rationales.D: Oral fluids increase aspiration risk when swallowing and cough are impaired.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 38-year-old male admitted 2 weeks after Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis with symmetric ascending lower-extremity weakness and paresthesias.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Absent patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes, 2/5 strength in lower extremities, 4/5 strength in upper extremities.

laboratory_results.CSF analysis: Albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein 112 mg/dL, normal WBC 2/mm3)

questions.stem: A client with Guillain-Barré syndrome has ascending weakness. Which new finding most strongly indicates progression toward respiratory failure and requires immediate escalation?

options.text: A declining vital capacity with a weaker cough and difficulty counting to ten in one breath
Bilateral absent ankle reflexes with preserved cough and stable respiratory measurements
Burning paresthesia in both feet that is unchanged from the previous assessment
Mild constipation after reduced mobility

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Serial respiratory mechanics and bulbar/cough function identify impending ventilatory failure; deterioration requires urgent airway planning.
rationales.B: Areflexia is expected in GBS but does not by itself indicate imminent respiratory failure.
rationales.C: Stable sensory symptoms do not indicate acute respiratory deterioration.
rationales.D: Constipation is important to manage but is not the immediate life threat.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 73-year-old male with Parkinson disease admitted for a minor urologic procedure.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Resting pill-rolling tremor of right hand, bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, shuffling gait.
provider_orders: Administer Parkinson medications strictly on home schedule

questions.stem: A client with Parkinson disease reports that carbidopa-levodopa takes longer to work after breakfast. The meal is high in protein. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.text: Discuss consistent dose timing and separating doses from high-protein meals when directed, without reducing total protein intake independently
Eliminate protein from the diet because it permanently blocks levodopa absorption
Take each dose only when tremors become severe to prevent tolerance
Crush all extended-release tablets and mix them with a protein shake

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Dietary amino acids can compete with levodopa transport; consistent timing and individualized meal scheduling may improve response while preserving nutrition.
rationales.B: Protein is essential and should not be eliminated; timing rather than global restriction is considered.
rationales.C: Levodopa is generally scheduled to maintain symptom control, not taken only when symptoms peak.
rationales.D: Extended-release formulations should not be crushed, and a protein shake may worsen competition for absorption.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 20-year-old college student brought to the emergency department with severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and fever.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, petechial rash on lower extremities, drowsy.
provider_orders: STAT blood cultures followed by empiric IV antibiotics

questions.stem: A client presents with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. Bacterial meningitis is suspected. Which action should the nurse implement immediately while diagnostic evaluation proceeds?

options.text: Initiate droplet precautions and ensure prompt antimicrobial treatment is not delayed for nonessential procedures
Place the client in airborne isolation and defer antibiotics until the culture results are final
Use contact precautions only because transmission occurs through contaminated surfaces
Wait for lumbar puncture results before initiating any isolation measures

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Droplet precautions are indicated for suspected meningococcal disease and many bacterial meningitis protocols; urgent antibiotics should not be unnecessarily delayed.
rationales.B: Airborne isolation is not the routine precaution for meningococcal meningitis, and culture results take time.
rationales.C: Contact precautions alone are insufficient for droplet-transmitted pathogens.
rationales.D: Isolation should begin on suspicion, not after results return.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 51-year-old female in the neuro-ICU day 5 following endovascular coiling of a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Previously alert and oriented, now becomes lethargic with new left arm drift.

diagnostic_results.Transcranial Doppler: Elevated mean flow velocity in right middle cerebral artery

medications: Nimodipine 60 mg via NG tube every 4 hours

questions.stem: A client is receiving nimodipine after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage. Which outcome best explains the purpose of this medication?

options.text: Reduced risk of delayed cerebral ischemic deficits associated with post-hemorrhagic vasospasm
Immediate reduction of intracranial pressure by osmotic diuresis
Prevention of rebleeding by directly sealing the aneurysm
Dissolution of the subarachnoid clot to restore cerebral blood flow

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Nimodipine improves neurologic outcomes by reducing delayed ischemic deficits after aneurysmal SAH; it does not directly reverse the bleed.
rationales.B: It is not an osmotic agent and does not directly lower ICP.
rationales.C: Aneurysm securing, not nimodipine, addresses the source of rebleeding.
rationales.D: Nimodipine is not a thrombolytic and does not dissolve the clot.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 82-year-old male with moderate Alzheimer disease admitted to a medical unit for cellulitis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Becomes increasingly agitated and disoriented at 1830, attempting to climb out of bed looking for his car keys.

questions.stem: A client with Alzheimer disease becomes more restless each evening, repeatedly attempts to leave the unit, and is more distressed in a noisy dayroom. Which nursing approach is best?

options.text: Reduce environmental stimulation, maintain a predictable evening routine, and assess for unmet needs such as pain, toileting, or fatigue
Confront the client firmly with the correct date and insist that the client remain seated
Use a physical restraint at the start of each evening to prevent wandering
Keep the lights dim and the room completely dark to encourage sleep

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: A calm, structured environment and assessment for triggers can reduce sundowning-related distress while preserving safety.
rationales.B: Repeated confrontation can increase anxiety and does not address the cause of the behavior.
rationales.C: Restraints can worsen agitation and cause harm; use individualized least-restrictive safety measures.
rationales.D: Complete darkness may increase disorientation and fall risk; lighting should support orientation and safe mobility.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 35-year-old female with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS) discharged after IV methylprednisolone therapy for an acute optic neuritis flare.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Visual acuity improving, mild lower extremity spasticity, reports chronic afternoon fatigue.
medications: Baclofen 10 mg PO three times daily

questions.stem: A client with multiple sclerosis is planning home routines after discharge. Which strategies are appropriate to reduce symptom exacerbation and preserve function? Select all that apply.

options.text: Schedule demanding activities during periods of greatest energy and include planned rest periods
Use cooling strategies and avoid overheating when heat worsens symptoms
Continue prescribed exercise within tolerance to maintain strength and mobility
Stop all physical activity whenever fatigue occurs, even after rest improves symptoms
Report new or rapidly worsening neurologic symptoms rather than assuming every change is a routine flare

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Energy conservation helps manage fatigue without abandoning activity.
rationales.B: Heat can temporarily worsen neurologic symptoms; cooling and avoiding overheating may help.
rationales.C: Appropriate exercise supports function and should be individualized to tolerance.
rationales.D: Complete inactivity promotes deconditioning; balance activity with rest.
rationales.E: New symptoms may reflect relapse, infection, or another urgent condition and warrant assessment.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 42-year-old female who underwent a diagnostic lumbar puncture 2 hours ago.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Alert and oriented, puncture dressing clean and dry, reports a new throbbing frontal headache that intensifies when sitting up and improves when lying flat.
medications: Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours PRN

questions.stem: Several hours after a lumbar puncture, the client reports a severe headache that worsens when sitting and improves when lying flat. There is no fever, neck rigidity, or focal deficit. Which intervention is most appropriate initially?

options.text: Assist the client to lie flat for comfort, encourage fluids if not contraindicated, and notify the provider if symptoms persist or worsen
Keep the client upright and encourage walking to accelerate cerebrospinal-fluid replacement
Administer an anticoagulant to prevent a post-procedure clot
Perform repeated lumbar punctures to equalize cerebrospinal-fluid pressure

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: A positional headache is consistent with post-dural puncture headache; supportive measures and provider notification guide further management, including possible blood patch.
rationales.B: Upright posture typically worsens the headache.
rationales.C: Anticoagulation is not indicated and may increase procedural bleeding risk.
rationales.D: Repeated puncture is not a treatment and could worsen the leak.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 24-year-old female with type 1 diabetes mellitus admitted to the ICU step-down unit with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Lethargic, dry mucous membranes, Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath odor.
medications: Regular insulin IV infusion ordered at 0.1 units/kg/hr
provider_orders: DKA protocol: IV fluids, potassium replacement, regular insulin infusion

questions.stem: A client with DKA has received initial isotonic fluid. Potassium is 3.1 mEq/L, glucose is 520 mg/dL, and an insulin infusion is prescribed. What should the nurse do before starting insulin?

options.text: Hold insulin temporarily and initiate prescribed potassium replacement with close ECG and laboratory monitoring
Start insulin at the full rate because glucose is critically elevated and potassium will rise
Administer sodium bicarbonate before checking the serum potassium again
Restrict IV fluids until the potassium concentration returns to normal

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly; when potassium is below 3.3 mEq/L, replacement is required before insulin to reduce life-threatening dysrhythmia risk.
rationales.B: Starting insulin with significant hypokalemia can worsen the deficit and precipitate arrhythmias.
rationales.C: Bicarbonate is not routine DKA therapy and can further lower potassium; treatment depends on severe acidosis criteria.
rationales.D: Fluid resuscitation remains important; restriction does not correct the potassium deficit or DKA.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 33-year-old female with untreated Graves disease admitted after a motor vehicle collision with acute thyroid storm.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Agitated, delirious, profuse diaphoresis, warm flushed skin, palpable thyroid bruit.

diagnostic_results.ECG: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response

provider_orders: Administer PTU 1 hour prior to Lugol iodine solution

questions.stem: A client with thyroid storm is prescribed propylthiouracil (PTU), followed by potassium iodide. Why should PTU be given first?

options.text: Blocking new thyroid hormone synthesis before iodine administration reduces the risk that iodine will be used as substrate for additional hormone production
PTU increases iodine absorption so potassium iodide can rapidly enter the thyroid gland
Potassium iodide inactivates PTU if both medications are administered together
PTU prevents the hypotension caused by potassium iodide

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Thionamides are administered before iodine so organification and new hormone synthesis are blocked before iodine is supplied.
rationales.B: PTU does not work by increasing iodine absorption.
rationales.C: The sequencing is intended to block hormone synthesis before iodine is given, not to prevent direct chemical inactivation.
rationales.D: The sequence is based on thyroid hormone synthesis, not prevention of hypotension.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 44-year-old female with primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) brought to the emergency department after 2 days of viral gastroenteritis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Confused, severe generalized weakness, hyperpigmentation over knuckles and buccal mucosa, poor skin turgor.
medications: Hydrocortisone sodium succinate 100 mg IV push STAT

questions.stem: A client with primary adrenal insufficiency presents with vomiting, profound weakness, and hypotension. Which laboratory pattern most strongly supports adrenal crisis?

options.text: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia
Hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and hyperglycemia
Hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and hypercalcemia
Hypernatremia, hyperkalemia, and hyperglycemia

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Cortisol and aldosterone deficiency can produce sodium loss, potassium retention, volume depletion, and low glucose.
rationales.B: This pattern is opposite to the usual mineralocorticoid-deficient state.
rationales.C: Hypokalemia is not expected in primary adrenal crisis.
rationales.D: Hypernatremia and hyperglycemia do not fit the typical crisis pattern.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 60-year-old male with small-cell lung cancer admitted with worsening confusion and lethargy.
clinical_scenario.assessment: No peripheral edema, normal skin turgor, oriented to person only.

diagnostic_results.Head CT: Mild diffuse cerebral edema, no mass

medications: 3% Sodium Chloride IV infusion at 30 mL/hr

questions.stem: A client with severe symptomatic hyponatremia is receiving carefully controlled hypertonic saline. Why must the nurse monitor sodium closely and avoid overly rapid correction?

options.text: Rapid correction can cause osmotic demyelination, with potentially irreversible neurologic injury
Slow correction causes cerebral edema to worsen indefinitely and must be avoided
Frequent sodium checks prevent hyperkalemia caused by saline infusion
Rapid correction causes acute renal failure by precipitating sodium crystals

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Chronic hyponatremia allows brain adaptation; rapid rise in serum sodium can cause osmotic demyelination, so correction limits and monitoring are essential.
rationales.B: The goal is controlled correction; overly rapid correction is the major neurologic hazard.
rationales.C: Sodium monitoring is directed at correction rate and neurologic safety, not prevention of hyperkalemia.
rationales.D: Sodium does not precipitate as crystals in this manner; the concern is osmotic injury.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 46-year-old female 6 hours post-total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Mild anterior neck swelling, reports tingling around her lips and fingertips.
medications: Calcium gluconate 1 g IV ordered PRN symptomatic hypocalcemia
provider_orders: Keep tracheostomy tray and suction at bedside

questions.stem: Four hours after thyroidectomy, a client reports tingling around the mouth and fingertips. The nurse notes intermittent hand spasms. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assess for hypocalcemia and obtain the prescribed calcium level
Keep emergency airway equipment available and assess for laryngospasm or stridor
Notify the provider promptly and anticipate prescribed IV calcium for symptomatic hypocalcemia
Massage the neck incision firmly to relieve the muscle spasms
Reassure the client that these findings are an expected effect of anesthesia and need no follow-up

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm suggest hypocalcemia from parathyroid injury or stunning.
rationales.B: Hypocalcemia can cause laryngospasm; airway readiness is essential.
rationales.C: Symptomatic hypocalcemia may require prompt IV calcium under monitoring.
rationales.D: Pressure or massage over the incision is not an appropriate treatment and may cause harm.
rationales.E: These are warning signs, not routine anesthesia effects.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 49-year-old male 24 hours post-transsphenoidal hypophysectomy for a pituitary macroadenoma.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Intense thirst, dry skin, urine output 450 mL/hr for the past 3 consecutive hours, urine pale and watery.
medications: Desmopressin (DDAVP) 1 mcg IV PRN urine output > 250 mL/hr for 2 consecutive hours

questions.stem: A client with central diabetes insipidus has urine output of 700 mL/hr, serum sodium of 154 mEq/L, and increasing thirst. Which nursing action has the highest priority?

options.text: Assess hemodynamic status and fluid deficit, replace fluids as prescribed, and administer desmopressin as ordered
Restrict fluids to reduce urinary output until serum sodium normalizes
Administer a loop diuretic to reduce free-water loss
Delay treatment until urine osmolality results confirm the diagnosis

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
