rationales.A: The client is losing large volumes of free water and is hypernatremic; prompt volume assessment, replacement, and antidiuretic therapy are central.
rationales.B: Fluid restriction worsens dehydration and hypernatremia.
rationales.C: Loop diuretics can increase water loss and are not treatment for central DI.
rationales.D: Treatment should not be unnecessarily delayed when the clinical picture is clear and the client is deteriorating.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 67-year-old male admitted with oliguric acute kidney injury secondary to rhabdomyolysis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Generalized muscle weakness, urine output 15 mL/hr (dark tea-colored).

diagnostic_results.12-lead ECG: Tall peaked T waves and widened QRS complexes

medications: Regular insulin 10 units IV with 50% dextrose 50 mL IV

questions.stem: A client with acute kidney injury has potassium of 6.8 mEq/L and peaked T waves. Which prescribed medication should the nurse administer first to reduce the immediate risk of a fatal dysrhythmia?

options.text: IV calcium gluconate
Regular insulin with dextrose
Nebulized albuterol
Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: IV calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane and is the immediate priority when hyperkalemia produces ECG changes; it does not lower serum potassium.
rationales.B: Insulin with dextrose shifts potassium intracellularly but does not provide immediate membrane stabilization.
rationales.C: Albuterol can shift potassium intracellularly but is adjunctive and not a substitute for calcium with ECG changes.
rationales.D: Potassium binders remove potassium over time and are not the immediate intervention for ECG toxicity.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 63-year-old female with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) admitted for pneumonia; has a mature left forearm arteriovenous (AV) fistula.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Palpable vibration (thrill) and audible swishing sound (bruit) over left forearm fistula.
medications: Cefepime 1 g IV every 24 hours (renally dosed)
Sevelamer carbonate 800 mg PO with meals
provider_orders: Limb alert wristband on left arm

questions.stem: A client with a left-arm arteriovenous fistula is admitted for pneumonia. Which nursing actions protect the access? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assess for a palpable thrill and audible bruit according to policy
Use the opposite arm for blood pressure measurements and venipuncture
Avoid constrictive clothing or prolonged pressure over the fistula
Apply a tight dressing over the access whenever the client sleeps
Report loss of thrill or bruit immediately

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: A thrill and bruit help indicate fistula patency; changes require prompt assessment.
rationales.B: Blood pressure cuffs and venipuncture can injure or compromise the access.
rationales.C: External compression can impair blood flow and thrombose the fistula.
rationales.D: Routine tight dressing is contraindicated because it can obstruct flow.
rationales.E: Loss of thrill or bruit may indicate thrombosis and requires urgent escalation.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 55-year-old male performing continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) admitted with abdominal pain and low-grade fever.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Diffuse abdominal tenderness with mild rebound, peritoneal dialysis effluent bag is cloudy.
provider_orders: Send peritoneal effluent for cell count, Gram stain, and culture

questions.stem: During peritoneal dialysis, the client reports new diffuse abdominal discomfort. The drained dialysate is cloudy. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Obtain a specimen of the effluent for cell count and culture using aseptic technique and notify the dialysis team promptly
Increase the dwell time and reassess the clarity of the next exchange
Add an over-the-counter antacid to the dialysate to reduce irritation
Discard the cloudy effluent and document it as an expected finding after several exchanges

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Cloudy effluent with abdominal pain is peritonitis until proven otherwise; obtain specimens and initiate prompt evaluation and treatment.
rationales.B: Delaying assessment can worsen infection and compromise treatment.
rationales.C: Nothing should be added to dialysate without an explicit sterile prescription.
rationales.D: Cloudiness is not an expected benign finding and must be investigated.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 70-year-old male 4 hours post-transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) with a 3-way indwelling Foley catheter and continuous bladder irrigation (CBI).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports severe lower abdominal bladder spasms and an intense urge to void; drainage tubing shows dark red fluid with clots and slow outflow.
medications: Belladonna and opium suppository PRN bladder spasms
provider_orders: Titrate CBI rate to maintain light pink to clear urine output

questions.stem: Four hours after TURP, the client reports severe suprapubic pressure. The bladder is distended, drainage has slowed, and clots are visible in the tubing. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess the tubing for kinks or obstruction and restore prescribed continuous bladder irrigation patency according to protocol
Increase the irrigation rate to maximum without assessing the outflow
Clamp the catheter for 30 minutes to allow the bladder to rest
Remove the three-way catheter and insert a smaller catheter to improve drainage

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Bladder distention and reduced outflow suggest obstruction; assess the system and restore patency per protocol, including prescribed irrigation management.
rationales.B: Increasing inflow without ensuring outflow can worsen bladder distention and injury.
rationales.C: Clamping the catheter worsens retention and pressure.
rationales.D: Removing or exchanging a fresh postoperative catheter risks trauma and should be directed by the urology team.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 56-year-old female admitted with severe intractable vomiting and high-output nasogastric tube suctioning for 3 days.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Lethargic, muscle cramping, shallow respirations.
medications: 0.9% Sodium Chloride with 40 mEq KCl/L IV at 125 mL/hr
provider_orders: Replace NG output mL-for-mL with 0.45% NaCl + 20 mEq KCl/L

questions.stem: A client with COPD is drowsier than earlier. ABG results are pH 7.29, PaCO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 29 mEq/L, and PaO2 58 mmHg. How should the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: Acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia
Fully compensated metabolic alkalosis with expected oxygenation
Uncompensated metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
Acute respiratory alkalosis with severe hypoxemia

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: The low pH and elevated PaCO2 indicate respiratory acidosis; elevated bicarbonate suggests some chronic renal compensation, while low PaO2 indicates hypoxemia.
rationales.B: The pH is acidemic and PaCO2 is elevated, not a primary metabolic alkalosis.
rationales.C: The primary change is increased CO2, not reduced bicarbonate.
rationales.D: Respiratory alkalosis would have a low PaCO2 and elevated pH.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 50-year-old male with alcohol use disorder admitted for acute pancreatitis and refractory hypokalemia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes (3+), positive Trousseau sign, tremors.

diagnostic_results.Telemetry: Prolonged QT interval with occasional non-sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (torsades de pointes)

medications: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV in 100 mL D5W over 1 hour

questions.stem: A client with persistent hypokalemia has a magnesium level of 1.1 mg/dL despite repeated potassium replacement. Why should the nurse anticipate magnesium replacement?

options.text: Magnesium deficiency promotes renal potassium wasting, making hypokalemia difficult to correct until magnesium is restored
Magnesium replacement directly converts intracellular potassium into serum potassium
Low magnesium prevents potassium absorption from the gastrointestinal tract only
Magnesium is given to prevent calcium from binding potassium in the bloodstream

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Hypomagnesemia increases renal potassium loss and can make hypokalemia refractory to replacement.
rationales.B: Magnesium does not directly move potassium into serum in this way.
rationales.C: The mechanism is not limited to gastrointestinal absorption; renal wasting is important.
rationales.D: Calcium-potassium binding is not the relevant mechanism.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 58-year-old male with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis admitted with confusion, inverted sleep-wake cycle, and asterixis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Jaundiced sclera, spider angiomas, moderate ascites, flapping tremor when wrists are dorsiflexed.

diagnostic_results.Abdominal Ultrasound: Nodular cirrhotic liver, patent portal vein, moderate ascites

medications: Lactulose 30 mL PO every 2 hours until bowel movement, then titrate
provider_orders: Titrate lactulose to achieve 2 to 3 soft stools per day

questions.stem: A client with hepatic encephalopathy is receiving lactulose. Which finding best indicates that the treatment is achieving its intended effect without excessive fluid loss?

options.text: The client is more alert and has approximately 2–3 soft stools per day
The client has no bowel movement for 48 hours and increasing confusion
The client develops 8 watery stools daily with orthostatic hypotension
The serum ammonia rises while the client becomes increasingly somnolent

rationales.summary: Interpret the evolving clinical data and select the safest evidence-informed nursing response.
rationales.A: Lactulose reduces intestinal ammonia absorption; improved mentation and a target of a few soft stools daily indicate response.
rationales.B: Constipation can reduce treatment effectiveness and worsening confusion suggests deterioration.
rationales.C: Excessive diarrhea can cause dehydration and electrolyte disturbances; the dose requires reassessment.
rationales.D: Rising ammonia with worsening mental status suggests inadequate response or another cause requiring evaluation.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 46-year-old male admitted with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and persistent nausea/vomiting.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Guarding in epigastrium, hypoactive bowel sounds, bluish discoloration around umbilicus (Cullen sign).

diagnostic_results.Abdominal CT: Edematous pancreas with peripancreatic fluid collections

medications: Lactated Ringer IV infusion at 200 mL/hr
Hydromorphone 1 mg IV every 3 hours PRN severe pain

questions.stem: A client with acute pancreatitis has persistent vomiting, severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, and rising hematocrit. Which interventions are appropriate during the initial phase? Select all that apply.

options.text: Administer prescribed isotonic IV fluids and reassess perfusion, urine output, and respiratory status
Provide prescribed analgesia and reassess pain and sedation
Monitor for hypoxemia, increasing work of breathing, and signs of systemic complications
Offer a high-fat meal to stimulate pancreatic enzyme release and restore nutrition
Maintain NPO status only while vomiting or severe symptoms persist, then advance nutrition as clinically appropriate

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: Early fluid resuscitation addresses intravascular depletion, but must be titrated with frequent reassessment to avoid overload.
rationales.B: Pain control is important and should be monitored for therapeutic and adverse effects.
rationales.C: Pancreatitis can cause systemic inflammation, pleural effusion, and respiratory failure; respiratory monitoring is essential.
rationales.D: High-fat meals stimulate pancreatic secretion and are inappropriate during acute illness.
rationales.E: Feeding should be individualized; prolonged unnecessary fasting is not beneficial, but oral intake may be deferred during uncontrolled vomiting or severe symptoms.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 64-year-old male admitted to the ICU step-down unit with massive hematemesis from bleeding esophageal varices.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Pale, diaphoretic, drowsy, coughing up bright red blood.

diagnostic_results.History: Portal hypertension secondary to hepatitis C cirrhosis

medications: Octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus followed by 50 mcg/hr infusion
provider_orders: Prepare for emergent esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with variceal band ligation

questions.stem: A client arrives with hematemesis, tachycardia, cool extremities, and a blood pressure of 86/54 mmHg. An emergent endoscopy is planned. Which intervention takes priority before transport?

options.text: Establish large-bore IV access, begin prescribed resuscitation, and prepare blood products while reassessing hemodynamic response
Administer the prescribed oral proton-pump inhibitor with a sip of water and transport immediately
Obtain a stool occult-blood sample before initiating IV therapy
Give a sedative to reduce anxiety and prevent further hematemesis

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: The client has signs of hemorrhagic shock; circulation stabilization, access, blood-product readiness, and ongoing reassessment precede transport when feasible.
rationales.B: Oral medication is inappropriate in active hematemesis and does not address shock.
rationales.C: A stool test does not change immediate management and delays resuscitation.
rationales.D: Sedation can worsen hypotension and airway risk; stabilization is the priority.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 54-year-old female 2 days post-sigmoid colostomy creation for diverticular perforation.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Stoma in left lower quadrant is moist, beefy red, and slightly edematous; small amount of serosanguinous fluid in pouch.
medications: Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours PRN
provider_orders: Ostomy nurse consult and client teaching

questions.stem: A client is 8 hours after creation of a new colostomy. Which stoma finding requires immediate notification of the surgeon?

options.text: A dusky purple, cool stoma with delayed capillary refill
A moist, pink-red stoma with mild edema
Scant blood-tinged mucus on the pouch during the first postoperative day
No formed stool in the pouch during the first several hours after surgery

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: A dusky, cool stoma with poor perfusion suggests ischemia or necrosis and requires urgent evaluation.
rationales.B: Mild edema and a moist pink-red appearance are expected early postoperative findings.
rationales.C: Small amounts of blood-tinged mucus can occur after surgery.
rationales.D: Bowel function may take time to return; absence of formed stool in the first hours is not by itself evidence of compromise.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 61-year-old male receiving a unit of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) for symptomatic anemia (Hgb 6.8 g/dL).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Fifteen minutes after starting the transfusion, the client reports chills, lower back pain, and chest tightness.

questions.stem: Fifteen minutes after a PRBC transfusion begins, the client develops chills, back pain, fever, tachycardia, and hypotension. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.

items: Disconnect the blood tubing at the hub and infuse 0.9% sodium chloride through new IV tubing
Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and vital signs while notifying the provider and blood bank
Return the blood bag and tubing to the blood bank and collect post-transfusion blood and urine samples

correct_response: Disconnect the blood tubing at the hub and infuse 0.9% sodium chloride through new IV tubing
Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and vital signs while notifying the provider and blood bank
Return the blood bag and tubing to the blood bank and collect post-transfusion blood and urine samples

rationales.1: Stopping the transfusion prevents additional incompatible blood from entering the circulation.
rationales.2: New tubing prevents residual blood in the original tubing from infusing while maintaining access with normal saline.
rationales.3: Assess ABCs and hemodynamics and notify the provider and blood bank promptly.
rationales.4: Return the unit and tubing and obtain ordered specimens to investigate hemolysis and guide treatment.
rationales.summary: Suspected acute hemolytic reaction requires immediate cessation of the transfusion, preservation of IV access with new tubing, urgent assessment and notification, then investigation.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 48-year-old female receiving consolidation chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Fatigued, oral mucosa pink without lesions, central venous catheter dressing dry and intact.
provider_orders: Notify provider immediately for temperature >= 38.0 C (100.4 F)

questions.stem: A client receiving induction chemotherapy has an absolute neutrophil count of 300/mm³. Which protective measures should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.

options.text: Perform meticulous hand hygiene and require visitors with respiratory symptoms to defer visits
Monitor temperature and report a single oral temperature of 38.0°C (100.4°F) or higher promptly
Avoid rectal temperatures, suppositories, and rectal examinations
Allow fresh flowers and raw sprouts if the client washes hands before eating
Use meticulous central-line care and assess for subtle signs of infection

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: Hand hygiene and limiting exposure to ill contacts reduce infection risk.
rationales.B: Febrile neutropenia is an emergency; prompt reporting and evaluation are required.
rationales.C: Rectal procedures can injure mucosa and introduce organisms.
rationales.D: Fresh flowers and raw sprouts may carry organisms and are commonly restricted under neutropenic food-safety policies.
rationales.E: Central lines are a major infection source; meticulous care and surveillance are essential.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 52-year-old male with high-grade Burkitt lymphoma 24 hours after starting induction chemotherapy.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports muscle cramps, flank discomfort, and decreased urine output.

questions.stem: A client with high-grade lymphoma develops acute kidney injury 24 hours after chemotherapy. Which laboratory pattern most strongly supports tumor lysis syndrome?

options.text: Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and hypocalcemia
Hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypouricemia, and hypercalcemia
Hypernatremia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, and low uric acid
Hyponatremia, hypokalemia, low phosphate, and metabolic alkalosis

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: Rapid tumor-cell breakdown releases potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids; uric acid rises and phosphate binds calcium, causing hypocalcemia.
rationales.B: This is the opposite of the characteristic biochemical pattern.
rationales.C: These abnormalities do not reflect the release of intracellular tumor contents.
rationales.D: This pattern is not characteristic of tumor lysis syndrome.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 25-year-old male with sickle cell anemia admitted with severe bilateral femur and lower back pain (9/10) following a cold-weather trip.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Grimacing in pain, scleral icterus, extremities cool to touch.
provider_orders: Incentive spirometry every hour while awake

questions.stem: A client with sickle cell disease has severe limb pain, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, and no fever or respiratory symptoms. Which initial plan best addresses the vaso-occlusive episode?

options.text: Promptly provide prescribed opioid analgesia, encourage or administer appropriate hydration, and reassess oxygenation and pain response
Apply ice packs to the painful joints and restrict fluids to reduce tissue edema
Administer supplemental oxygen until saturation is 100% regardless of respiratory findings
Delay analgesia until radiographs confirm that no fracture is present

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: Rapid analgesia and appropriate hydration are central; monitor for acute chest syndrome and other complications while reassessing response.
rationales.B: Cold causes vasoconstriction and can worsen sickling; fluid restriction increases dehydration risk.
rationales.C: Oxygen is indicated for hypoxemia, not automatically to achieve 100% in a normoxic client.
rationales.D: Pain treatment should not be delayed for imaging when the presentation is consistent with vaso-occlusive crisis and no injury is suspected.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 32-year-old male 8 hours post-open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of a comminuted right tibial shaft fracture with a circumferential plaster cast.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports severe, escalating right lower leg pain (10/10) unrelieved by IV hydromorphone given 30 minutes ago; excruciating pain when the nurse passively dorsiflexes his right great toe; toes are tense and pale.
medications: Hydromorphone 1 mg IV every 3 hours PRN pain

questions.stem: Eight hours after tibial fixation, the client reports escalating pain despite opioid medication. Passive toe extension produces severe pain, and the affected compartment feels tense. Distal pulses remain palpable. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the orthopedic team immediately, keep the limb at heart level, and prepare for urgent compartment-pressure assessment or fasciotomy
Elevate the limb well above the heart and apply ice while waiting for the next analgesic dose
Reassure the client because palpable distal pulses exclude compartment syndrome
Loosen the external dressing if permitted by protocol and reassess later in the shift

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch are early warning signs; pulses may remain present until late. Urgent escalation is required and the limb should not be elevated above heart level.
rationales.B: High elevation can further reduce perfusion; ice and delay are inappropriate when compartment syndrome is suspected.
rationales.C: Pulses can remain palpable in compartment syndrome and do not exclude it.
rationales.D: Removing external constriction may be appropriate under protocol, but reassessment later delays definitive evaluation.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 40-year-old male weighing 80 kg brought to the burn center immediately after sustaining deep partial- and full-thickness thermal burns over 40% of his total body surface area (TBSA).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Alert, hoarse voice, singed nasal hairs, circumferential burns on anterior trunk and bilateral upper extremities.
provider_orders: Parkland formula fluid resuscitation: 4 mL x weight (kg) x %TBSA over 24 hours (half in first 8 hours)

questions.stem: A client weighs 80 kg and has burns over 40% TBSA. Using the Parkland estimate of 4 mL × kg × %TBSA, calculate the initial hourly rate for the first 8 hours after the time of injury. Assume the client arrives immediately after the burn. Enter a whole number in mL/hr.

rationales.summary: The Parkland estimate is 4 × 80 × 40 = 12,800 mL over 24 hours. Half, 6,400 mL, is given during the first 8 hours from the time of injury: 6,400 ÷ 8 = 800 mL/hr.
rationales.calculation: 4 mL × 80 kg × 40 = 12,800 mL. First-half volume = 6,400 mL. 6,400 mL ÷ 8 hours = 800 mL/hr. Adjust actual fluids to perfusion and urine-output response; the formula is an initial estimate.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 68-year-old female admitted with septic shock requiring continuous norepinephrine vasopressor support.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Warm flushed skin, capillary refill 3 seconds, central venous catheter in right internal jugular vein.
provider_orders: Start norepinephrine at 8 mcg/min and titrate to maintain MAP >= 65 mmHg

questions.stem: Norepinephrine is supplied as 4 mg in 250 mL D5W. The prescribed starting dose is 8 mcg/min. What pump rate delivers this dose? Enter a whole number in mL/hr.

rationales.summary: The concentration is 16 mcg/mL. A dose of 8 mcg/min equals 480 mcg/hr; 480 ÷ 16 = 30 mL/hr.
rationales.calculation: 4 mg = 4,000 mcg. 4,000 mcg ÷ 250 mL = 16 mcg/mL. 8 mcg/min × 60 = 480 mcg/hr. 480 ÷ 16 = 30 mL/hr.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 53-year-old male receiving intravenous vancomycin 1.5 g in 250 mL normal saline for MRSA bacteremia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Fifteen minutes into the infusion, the client develops bright red erythematous flushing over his face, neck, and upper chest with pruritus.
provider_orders: Infuse vancomycin over at least 90-120 minutes

questions.stem: During a vancomycin infusion, the client develops flushing and itching of the face and upper chest. There is no wheezing, angioedema, or hypotension. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop or pause the infusion, assess airway and hemodynamic status, and notify the prescriber about a likely infusion-related reaction
Continue the infusion at the same rate and administer an antihistamine after completion
Label the client as having an IgE-mediated anaphylactic allergy without further assessment
Administer epinephrine immediately despite stable airway and circulation

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: Flushing and pruritus during infusion suggest a rate-related vancomycin infusion reaction; stop or slow the infusion and assess severity before restarting at a slower rate as prescribed.
rationales.B: Continuing the same rate may worsen the reaction; antihistamine does not replace stopping and assessment.
rationales.C: A rate-related infusion reaction is not automatically an IgE-mediated allergy; document the observed reaction accurately.
rationales.D: Epinephrine is indicated for anaphylaxis with airway, breathing, or circulatory compromise, not routinely for isolated flushing with stable status.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 69-year-old female receiving intravenous gentamicin for complicated pyelonephritis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports new ringing in both ears and mild dizziness when sitting on the edge of the bed.
provider_orders: Draw peak and trough levels around third dose

questions.stem: A client receiving gentamicin reports new tinnitus and difficulty hearing high-pitched sounds. Creatinine has increased from 0.8 to 1.6 mg/dL. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hold the next dose and promptly notify the prescriber of possible ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity
Review drug levels, renal function, dose interval, and concurrent nephrotoxic medications
Document the change in hearing and arrange prompt hearing assessment as directed
Encourage the client to take an NSAID for discomfort and continue the antibiotic unchanged
Assume the symptoms are temporary and reassess only after the full course is completed

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: New auditory symptoms and rising creatinine are concerning toxicities; the next dose should not proceed without prescriber review.
rationales.B: Gentamicin exposure is affected by renal function and drug levels; other nephrotoxins increase risk.
rationales.C: Prompt documentation and assessment help determine severity and whether therapy must change.
rationales.D: NSAIDs can add renal risk and do not address ototoxicity.
rationales.E: Waiting until therapy ends risks permanent hearing injury and worsening renal damage.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 45-year-old female 2 hours post-abdominal hysterectomy receiving morphine via patient-controlled analgesia (PCA).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Unarousable to sternal rub, pinpoint pupils (1 mm), snoring respirations.
medications: Naloxone 0.4 mg IV PRN respiratory depression

questions.stem: After naloxone reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression, the client becomes alert and respiratory rate improves. Why must the nurse continue close respiratory and sedation monitoring?

options.text: Naloxone may wear off before the opioid, allowing recurrent respiratory depression
Naloxone causes permanent opioid receptor blockade for 24 hours
The initial response proves that the opioid has been fully eliminated
Recurrent respiratory depression occurs only when naloxone is administered intramuscularly

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: Naloxone's duration may be shorter than that of the opioid; repeated dosing or infusion and continued monitoring may be needed.
rationales.B: Naloxone does not provide a 24-hour blockade.
rationales.C: Reversal of symptoms does not mean the opioid has been eliminated.
rationales.D: Recurrence can occur after any route when the opioid outlasts naloxone.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 58-year-old female admitted with severe dehydration and hypokalemia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Alert, weak peripheral pulses, dry oral mucosa, peripheral IV catheter in left forearm.

diagnostic_results.ECG: Flattened T waves with prominent U waves

medications: Potassium chloride 40 mEq in 1,000 mL 0.9% Sodium Chloride IV at 125 mL/hr
provider_orders: Verify urine output >= 30 mL/hr prior to potassium infusion

questions.stem: The nurse receives an order for potassium chloride 10 mEq IV for a client with potassium 2.9 mEq/L. Which safety principle is essential?

options.text: Dilute and administer using an infusion pump at the prescribed rate; never give potassium chloride by IV push
Give the dose by slow IV push through a central line to reduce peripheral irritation
Add potassium to a hanging IV bag at the bedside and estimate the final concentration
Administer the dose rapidly if continuous cardiac monitoring is available

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: IV potassium must be diluted and infused at a controlled rate using an infusion pump; IV push can cause fatal dysrhythmias.
rationales.B: Central access does not make IV push potassium safe.
rationales.C: Potassium should be prepared and verified according to medication-safety policy, not added ad hoc to a hanging bag.
rationales.D: Monitoring does not make rapid administration safe; rate limits still apply.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 56-year-old male started on lisinopril 10 mg daily 3 weeks ago for stage 2 hypertension.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports a persistent, dry, nonproductive hacking cough that started 1 week ago; lungs clear, no fever or dyspnea.

questions.stem: A client taking lisinopril develops a persistent dry cough. There is no fever, wheezing, or evidence of infection. Which explanation and plan are most appropriate?

options.text: ACE inhibition reduces bradykinin breakdown; the prescriber may consider an angiotensin-receptor blocker if the cough is intolerable
The cough indicates immediate pulmonary edema and requires a loop diuretic
The client should double the lisinopril dose because cough reflects inadequate blood-pressure control
The cough is caused by potassium loss and should be treated with a potassium supplement

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: ACE inhibitors can cause a dry cough related to bradykinin accumulation; an ARB may be considered when clinically appropriate.
rationales.B: A dry cough alone without congestion findings does not establish pulmonary edema.
rationales.C: Increasing the dose will not reliably resolve the adverse effect and may worsen it.
rationales.D: The cough is not caused by potassium loss; supplementation without labs may be unsafe.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 37-year-old male taking oral phenytoin 100 mg three times daily for focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Mild gingival hyperplasia, gait steady, alert and oriented.
medications: Phenytoin 100 mg PO three times daily
provider_orders: Continue current dose and reinforce medication teaching

questions.stem: A client taking phenytoin long term is preparing for discharge. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maintain consistent dosing and do not stop the medication abruptly without prescriber guidance
Use meticulous oral hygiene and arrange regular dental care
Report rash, unusual bruising, fever, or signs of infection promptly
Stop the medication once seizure-free for one month
Discuss pregnancy planning and contraception because phenytoin has important fetal and drug-interaction risks

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: Abrupt withdrawal can precipitate seizures; dosing should remain consistent.
rationales.B: Phenytoin can cause gingival hyperplasia, making oral care important.
rationales.C: Rash may signal a serious reaction, and blood dyscrasias can occur; warning signs require prompt review.
rationales.D: Seizure control does not mean the disorder is cured; stopping suddenly is unsafe.
rationales.E: Phenytoin is teratogenic and interacts with hormonal contraceptives; individualized counseling is important.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 41-year-old female taking lithium carbonate for bipolar I disorder who developed viral gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhea.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Coarse hand tremors, slurred speech, ataxia, drowsiness.
medications: Lithium carbonate 300 mg PO three times daily

questions.stem: A client taking lithium begins a thiazide diuretic and develops vomiting and poor oral intake. The lithium level is elevated. Which mechanism best explains the increased toxicity risk?

options.text: Sodium and volume depletion increase renal lithium reabsorption, reducing lithium clearance
Thiazides bind lithium in the intestine and increase its absorption
Dehydration increases hepatic metabolism of lithium, producing a toxic metabolite
Lithium is primarily excreted in bile, and dehydration blocks biliary drainage

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: Lithium is handled by the kidneys similarly to sodium; volume and sodium depletion increase proximal reabsorption and reduce lithium clearance.
rationales.B: Thiazides increase toxicity mainly through renal sodium handling, not intestinal binding.
rationales.C: Lithium is not primarily hepatically metabolized into a toxic metabolite.
rationales.D: Lithium is renally eliminated, not primarily excreted in bile.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 51-year-old female receiving continuous total parenteral nutrition (TPN) via a right subclavian central venous catheter for severe Crohn enterocutaneous fistula.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Alert, central line dressing clean and dry; nurse notices the current TPN bag has 15 mL remaining and the new bag from pharmacy is delayed by 45 minutes.
medications: TPN (20% dextrose, amino acids, electrolytes) infusing at 85 mL/hr
provider_orders: Change TPN bag and tubing every 24 hours

questions.stem: A client receiving continuous central-line TPN is told that the replacement bag will be delayed by 90 minutes. The current bag is nearly empty. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Follow the prescribed interruption protocol and begin the ordered dextrose-containing solution at the TPN rate while notifying the appropriate team
Flush the central catheter with saline and leave it capped until the TPN arrives
Stop all IV fluids because brief interruption of TPN does not affect glucose
Increase the remaining TPN rate so the bag finishes just before the replacement arrives

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: Abrupt interruption of high-dextrose TPN can cause hypoglycemia; a prescribed dextrose solution may be used as a bridge with monitoring.
rationales.B: Leaving the client without carbohydrate can precipitate hypoglycemia; central-line handling must follow protocol.
rationales.C: Clients receiving continuous TPN may become hypoglycemic if it is stopped abruptly.
rationales.D: Increasing the rate risks hyperglycemia and fluid/electrolyte complications and does not safely bridge the delay.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 59-year-old male prescribed allopurinol 100 mg PO daily for chronic tophaceous gout.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Mild non-tender tophi on right olecranon; currently free of acute joint inflammation.

questions.stem: A client taking allopurinol for gout calls to report a new widespread rash and fever. Which instruction should the nurse provide?

options.text: Stop the medication and seek urgent medical assessment because a serious hypersensitivity reaction is possible
Continue the medication and take an antihistamine because rash is an expected sign that uric acid is falling
Take an extra dose to prevent an acute gout flare while the rash is present
Stop drinking water until the rash resolves to reduce renal excretion of the drug

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: Allopurinol can cause severe cutaneous adverse reactions; rash with systemic symptoms requires immediate discontinuation and urgent assessment.
rationales.B: A rash is not a therapeutic sign and may progress to a life-threatening reaction.
rationales.C: Additional exposure may worsen a severe hypersensitivity reaction.
rationales.D: Hydration is generally encouraged unless contraindicated; fluid restriction is not a treatment for rash.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 32-year-old G1P0 at 35 weeks gestation receiving intravenous magnesium sulfate at 2 g/hr for severe preeclampsia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Somnolent, absent patellar deep tendon reflexes, skin flushed.
medications: Magnesium sulfate 40 g in 1,000 mL LR at 50 mL/hr (2 g/hr)
provider_orders: Calcium gluconate 1 g IV at bedside

questions.stem: A client receiving magnesium sulfate for severe preeclampsia has absent deep-tendon reflexes, a respiratory rate of 8/min, and urine output of 20 mL/hr. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the magnesium infusion, support ventilation, summon urgent help, and prepare the prescribed calcium gluconate antidote
Reduce the infusion by half and reassess reflexes in 30 minutes
Administer another magnesium bolus because oliguria indicates inadequate seizure prophylaxis
Give naloxone to reverse magnesium-related respiratory depression

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: Absent reflexes, respiratory depression, and oliguria indicate magnesium toxicity; stop the infusion and support airway/breathing while preparing calcium gluconate.
rationales.B: Reducing the dose is insufficient when severe toxicity is present.
rationales.C: Additional magnesium can cause cardiac and respiratory arrest.
rationales.D: Naloxone reverses opioids, not magnesium; calcium gluconate is the antidote.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 34-year-old male taking clozapine 300 mg PO daily for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Presents to the outpatient clinic reporting a sore throat, malaise, and chills for 24 hours.

questions.stem: A client taking clozapine reports fever, sore throat, and mouth ulcers. The client appears fatigued. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Withhold the next dose and arrange urgent CBC with absolute neutrophil count and prescriber review
Reassure the client that these are common anticholinergic effects and continue treatment
Administer acetaminophen and wait for the next scheduled blood count
Increase the clozapine dose because infection can trigger recurrence of psychosis

rationales.summary: The correct response depends on the specific clinical cues and the immediate risk to the client.
rationales.A: Fever and sore throat may indicate severe neutropenia or agranulocytosis; urgent ANC assessment and treatment decisions are required.
rationales.B: These symptoms are not routine anticholinergic effects and may signal a life-threatening adverse reaction.
rationales.C: Symptomatic treatment alone can delay detection of agranulocytosis.
rationales.D: Increasing clozapine in possible neutropenia is unsafe.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 28-year-old G2P1 at 39 weeks gestation in active labor at 6 cm dilation, membranes artificially ruptured 20 minutes ago.
clinical_scenario.assessment: External fetal monitor shows a baseline FHR of 140 bpm with moderate variability, punctuated by abrupt V-shaped drops in FHR to 95 bpm lasting 25 seconds with rapid return to baseline.

questions.stem: The fetal monitor shows recurrent abrupt decreases in fetal heart rate from 145 to 90/min, with rapid return to baseline. The client is 6 cm dilated and membranes ruptured 20 minutes ago. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Reposition the client, assess for cord prolapse, and evaluate the tracing and fetal recovery
Increase the oxytocin infusion to shorten labor and reduce fetal exposure to contractions
Prepare for immediate cesarean birth without first assessing reversible causes
Administer oxygen by nonrebreather routinely while keeping the client supine

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Abrupt variable decelerations suggest cord compression; maternal repositioning and assessment for prolapse or other reversible causes are appropriate first steps.
rationales.B: Increasing uterine activity can worsen fetal stress and is not appropriate with recurrent decelerations.
rationales.C: Immediate operative birth may be needed if the tracing remains nonreassuring, but initial assessment and intrauterine resuscitative measures are indicated.
rationales.D: Routine oxygen is not recommended for a normoxic mother; supine positioning may worsen uteroplacental perfusion.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 30-year-old G4P4 45 minutes after vaginal delivery of a 4,350 g infant following prolonged oxytocin induction.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Perineal pad saturated with bright red blood and large clots within 15 minutes; uterine fundus palpated 3 cm above the umbilicus, boggy, and deviated to the right.
medications: Oxytocin 20 units in 1,000 mL LR infusing at 125 mL/hr

questions.stem: Forty-five minutes after birth, the client has heavy vaginal bleeding and a boggy uterus displaced to the right. Blood pressure is 92/58 mmHg and heart rate is 118/min. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Call for assistance, massage the fundus while supporting the lower uterine segment, and assess bladder distention
Administer methylergonovine before assessing blood pressure or contraindications
Assist the client to ambulate to the bathroom without additional assessment
Apply an ice pack to the perineum and recheck the fundus in 30 minutes

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: A boggy displaced uterus suggests atony with possible bladder distention; immediate fundal massage, assistance, and rapid hemorrhage response are priorities.
rationales.B: Methylergonovine may be contraindicated with hypertension and should not precede immediate assessment and first-line measures.
rationales.C: Ambulation is unsafe in a client with active hemorrhage and hemodynamic changes.
rationales.D: Ice may help perineal discomfort but does not treat uterine atony or hemorrhage.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 34-year-old G1P0 at 34 weeks gestation admitted with severe preeclampsia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports right upper quadrant epigastric pain, nausea, and visual scotomata; 2+ pitting pedal edema.
medications: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading dose then 2 g/hr
provider_orders: Prepare for delivery after maternal stabilization

questions.stem: A client with severe preeclampsia develops right-upper-quadrant pain, nausea, falling platelets, and elevated liver enzymes. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Institute seizure precautions and maintain a low-stimulation environment
Assess for worsening hepatic involvement and report increasing right-upper-quadrant or epigastric pain promptly
Monitor blood pressure closely during prescribed IV antihypertensive therapy
Perform repeated deep abdominal palpation to determine liver enlargement
Prepare for possible urgent birth and blood-product support based on maternal and fetal status

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Severe preeclampsia carries seizure risk; safety and reduced stimulation are appropriate.
rationales.B: Pain may signal hepatic involvement or subcapsular hematoma and requires prompt escalation.
rationales.C: Frequent blood-pressure monitoring is needed during IV antihypertensive treatment to avoid excessive reduction and detect persistent severe hypertension.
rationales.D: Repeated deep palpation is not indicated and may cause harm when hepatic complications are suspected.
rationales.E: HELLP or worsening severe features may require expedited birth and blood-product readiness depending on labs and clinical status.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 31-year-old G3P2 at 33 weeks gestation brought to labor and delivery triage with sudden onset of painless, bright red vaginal bleeding.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Uterus is soft, relaxed, and nontender; fetal head is high and floating.

questions.stem: A pregnant client at 33 weeks presents with painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. Placental location is not yet known. Which assessment must the nurse avoid until placenta previa has been excluded?

options.text: Digital vaginal examination
External fetal heart-rate monitoring
Ultrasound assessment of placental location
Maternal vital signs and assessment of bleeding amount

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Digital cervical examination can disrupt a placenta previa and precipitate severe hemorrhage.
rationales.B: External fetal monitoring is appropriate to assess fetal status.
rationales.C: Ultrasound is used to determine placental location.
rationales.D: Maternal assessment and quantification of bleeding are essential.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 2-hour-old term male infant born to a mother with gestational diabetes mellitus; birth weight 4,280 g (LGA).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Jittery extremities, weak high-pitched cry, mild hypotonia.

questions.stem: A 2-hour-old infant of a diabetic mother is jittery. Point-of-care glucose is 32 mg/dL. The infant is awake, has a coordinated suck, and has no respiratory distress. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Initiate prompt feeding and follow the neonatal hypoglycemia protocol for repeat glucose and escalation if it remains low
Observe without feeding because jitteriness is common during transition after birth
Give sterile water by syringe and repeat the glucose at the next routine assessment
Begin IV dextrose immediately without attempting feeding or following the newborn protocol

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: An asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic infant who can feed may receive prompt feeding per protocol, with timely recheck and escalation for persistent or severe hypoglycemia.
rationales.B: Jitteriness may be a symptom of hypoglycemia and requires action.
rationales.C: Water does not correct neonatal hypoglycemia and can be harmful.
rationales.D: IV dextrose is indicated for severe symptoms, inability to feed, or failure of initial treatment per protocol; it is not automatically first for every stable infant.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 38-hour-old term female newborn receiving overhead LED phototherapy for unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Jaundiced skin over face and upper chest, vigorous suck, 4 wet diapers and 2 transitional stools in past 24 hours.

questions.stem: A term newborn is receiving phototherapy. Which nursing actions support treatment effectiveness and reduce complications? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maximize exposed skin while maintaining appropriate eye protection according to the device and policy
Monitor temperature, hydration, feeding, and urine/stool output
Remove eye protection during feeding and care to assess the eyes and support interaction
Apply oil-based lotion before each session to prevent skin dryness
Verify irradiance and distance according to the equipment instructions and monitor bilirubin as ordered

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Adequate skin exposure improves treatment while eye protection is used according to device guidance.
rationales.B: Phototherapy increases insensible water loss; temperature, hydration, and output require monitoring.
rationales.C: Brief removal during care allows eye assessment and bonding while maintaining safe protection during exposure.
rationales.D: Oils and lotions may alter heat absorption or cause skin injury and should not be applied unless specifically directed.
rationales.E: Correct equipment setup and serial bilirubin measurement ensure effective and safe therapy.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 26-year-old G1P1 postpartum client 12 hours after an uncomplicated vaginal birth.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Fundus firm at umbilicus, lochia rubra moderate, perineum intact.
medications: Rho(D) immune globulin 300 mcg IM ordered
provider_orders: Administer Rho(D) immune globulin within 72 hours of delivery

questions.stem: A postpartum client is Rh-negative and has not been sensitized. The newborn is Rh-positive. Which explanation best describes the purpose of Rho(D) immune globulin?

options.text: It prevents maternal sensitization by clearing fetal Rh-positive cells from the maternal circulation before an immune response develops
It treats hemolysis that is already occurring in the newborn
It changes the mother's red blood cells to Rh-positive
It provides lifelong immunity against all future blood-group incompatibilities

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Rho(D) immune globulin prevents formation of maternal anti-D antibodies after exposure to Rh-positive fetal cells.
rationales.B: It does not treat neonatal hemolytic disease once present.
rationales.C: It does not change maternal blood type.
rationales.D: It is specific to preventing Rh(D) sensitization and does not prevent all blood-group incompatibilities.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 29-year-old G2P1 at 38 weeks gestation in labor; spontaneous rupture of membranes occurs during a contraction.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Fetal heart rate abruptly drops from 140 bpm to 65 bpm with prolonged bradycardia; on sterile vaginal inspection, a pulsating loop of umbilical cord is palpated in the vagina.

questions.stem: Immediately after membrane rupture, the nurse sees and palpates a pulsating umbilical cord below the presenting part. The fetal heart rate falls to 70/min. Which action is the priority while help is summoned?

options.text: Use a gloved hand to lift the presenting part off the cord and maintain that pressure until birth
Attempt to push the cord back above the presenting part and then reassess the fetal heart rate
Apply fundal pressure to accelerate descent of the presenting part
Place the client supine and wait for the obstetric provider before intervening

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Relieving compression of the prolapsed cord is the immediate priority; maintain elevation of the presenting part while preparing for expedited birth.
rationales.B: Do not attempt to replace the cord; manipulation can cause vasospasm and injury.
rationales.C: Fundal pressure worsens cord compression.
rationales.D: Waiting without relieving compression risks prolonged fetal hypoxia; positioning and urgent birth preparation occur concurrently.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 4-year-old unvaccinated boy brought to the emergency department with sudden high fever, severe sore throat, and muffled voice.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Sitting upright leaning forward with chin thrust out (tripod position), drooling saliva, inspiratory stridor, anxious expression.

laboratory_results.Pending: Defer blood draws until airway secured

diagnostic_results.Pending: Portable lateral neck X-ray at bedside if stable

medications: Ceftriaxone IV ordered once airway secured
provider_orders: Pediatric anesthesia and ENT STAT to bedside

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with fever, drooling, muffled voice, and tripod positioning is suspected of having epiglottitis. Which action should the nurse avoid?

options.text: Inspecting the throat with a tongue depressor or attempting to obtain a throat swab
Keeping the child calm and upright with a parent present
Summoning the airway team and preparing for controlled airway management
Providing oxygen in the least distressing manner the child will tolerate

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Throat manipulation can precipitate complete airway obstruction; avoid upsetting the child and prepare for controlled airway management.
rationales.B: Calm upright positioning reduces distress and helps maintain the airway.
rationales.C: Early expert airway planning is essential because obstruction can progress rapidly.
rationales.D: Oxygen may be offered gently without forcing a mask or procedure that agitates the child.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 3-year-old female admitted with 6 days of persistent high fever, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, cracked red lips, and polymorphous rash.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Irritable, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of hands and feet.
medications: Aspirin 80 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours initially, then low-dose 3-5 mg/kg/day
provider_orders: Serial echocardiograms at baseline, 2 weeks, and 6-8 weeks

questions.stem: A child with Kawasaki disease is receiving IVIG and aspirin. Which discharge instructions and monitoring priorities are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep scheduled cardiology follow-up and echocardiography appointments even if the fever resolves
Report chest pain, unusual fatigue, pallor, or signs of poor perfusion promptly
Discuss timing of live vaccines with the provider because IVIG can interfere with vaccine response
Give ibuprofen routinely with aspirin to improve antiplatelet action
Use comfort measures for oral discomfort and encourage fluids the child can tolerate

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Coronary artery complications may develop or persist after fever resolves; follow-up imaging is essential.
rationales.B: Cardiac symptoms or poor perfusion require prompt assessment.
rationales.C: IVIG can interfere with live vaccine response; timing should be coordinated with the provider.
rationales.D: Ibuprofen may increase bleeding risk and can interfere with aspirin's antiplatelet effect; it should not be added routinely.
rationales.E: Hydration and comfort measures support intake and recovery.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 5-week-old male infant admitted with forceful, non-bilious projectile vomiting immediately after every feeding for 4 days.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Hungry immediately after vomiting, sunken anterior fontanelle, visible left-to-right peristaltic waves across upper abdomen, palpable olive-shaped mass in right upper quadrant.
medications: 0.9% Sodium Chloride IV bolus followed by D5 0.45% NaCl with 20 mEq KCl/L
provider_orders: Correct fluid and electrolyte imbalances prior to laparoscopic pyloromyotomy

questions.stem: An infant with pyloric stenosis has persistent projectile vomiting, chloride 88 mEq/L, potassium 3.0 mEq/L, and metabolic alkalosis. Why should surgery be delayed until fluid and electrolyte abnormalities are corrected?

options.text: Volume depletion and alkalosis increase anesthetic risk, including postoperative apnea and dysrhythmias
Correction is needed to shrink the pyloric muscle and eliminate the need for surgery
Electrolyte correction prevents the infant from developing lactose intolerance after surgery
The alkalosis prevents the pylorus from relaxing during the procedure

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Dehydration, hypochloremia, hypokalemia, and alkalosis increase peri-anesthetic risk; stabilize before pyloromyotomy.
rationales.B: Fluid therapy does not reliably reverse the anatomic hypertrophy or replace surgery.
rationales.C: Lactose intolerance is not the reason for preoperative correction.
rationales.D: The primary concern is systemic anesthetic and cardiopulmonary risk, not pyloric relaxation.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 9-month-old male brought to the emergency department for episodic inconsolable crying where he draws his knees up to his abdomen every 15 minutes, followed by lethargy.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Sausage-shaped mass palpated in right upper quadrant; diaper contains dark red mucoid stool ('currant jelly' stool).

diagnostic_results.Abdominal Ultrasound: Classic 'target sign' (telescoping of ileum into cecum)

provider_orders: Prepare for ultrasound-guided hydrostatic/pneumatic enema reduction

questions.stem: An infant with suspected intussusception is awaiting an image-guided air enema. The infant suddenly passes a normal-appearing stool and becomes comfortable. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the radiology and surgical teams before the procedure because spontaneous reduction may have occurred and requires reassessment
Proceed with the enema without reporting the change because stool passage confirms obstruction
Offer a full feeding to determine whether the bowel remains patent
Cancel the procedure independently and discharge the infant if pain has stopped

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Symptoms may resolve after spontaneous reduction, but reassessment and confirmation are needed before proceeding with an enema.
rationales.B: Stool passage and symptom relief do not confirm persistent obstruction; the team must reassess.
rationales.C: Oral feeding is inappropriate until obstruction and procedure plans are clarified.
rationales.D: The nurse should not independently cancel the procedure or discharge; recurrence and complications remain possible.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 6-month-old infant with unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot hospitalized for bronchiolitis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: During phlebotomy, the infant begins crying vigorously and develops acute deep circumoral and generalized cyanosis with rapid breathing.

diagnostic_results.Echocardiogram: VSD, overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, RVH

medications: Morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV/subcutaneous PRN hypercyanotic spell

questions.stem: During a procedure, an infant with unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot develops a hypercyanotic spell. Place the interventions in priority order, recognizing that oxygen and emergency assistance should be provided promptly.

items: Place the infant immediately in the knee-chest position while calming the infant
Administer prescribed morphine sulfate to relax infundibular spasm and reduce agitation
Administer prescribed intravenous normal saline bolus to improve right ventricular filling and pulmonary blood flow

correct_response: Place the infant immediately in the knee-chest position while calming the infant
Administer prescribed morphine sulfate to relax infundibular spasm and reduce agitation
Administer prescribed intravenous normal saline bolus to improve right ventricular filling and pulmonary blood flow

rationales.1: Knee-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance and can reduce right-to-left shunting; calm handling limits oxygen demand.
rationales.2: Provide oxygen as tolerated while maintaining the position and summoning help.
rationales.3: Prescribed morphine can reduce agitation and infundibular spasm; monitor respiratory status closely.
rationales.4: A prescribed isotonic bolus may improve preload and pulmonary blood flow when indicated.
rationales.summary: A hypercyanotic spell requires immediate reduction of right-to-left shunting and oxygen demand, followed by prescribed medication and fluid support while escalating to the provider.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 3-month-old infant 4 hours post-cheiloplasty (cleft lip repair).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Lip suture line intact with Logan bow/protective dressing, mild serous oozing, infant awake and sucking on fingers.
medications: Acetaminophen 15 mg/kg PO/PR every 6 hours PRN pain
provider_orders: Clear liquids via specialized syringe/Haberman feeder

questions.stem: Four hours after cleft-lip repair, the infant is crying and rubbing the face. Which nursing action best protects the repair while addressing comfort?

options.text: Position supine or side-lying as prescribed, use ordered elbow restraints with frequent skin and circulation checks, and soothe without placing objects against the incision
Place the infant prone so secretions drain away from the incision
Offer a pacifier to reduce crying and prevent stress on the repair
Clean the incision vigorously with dry gauze after each feeding

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Positioning and carefully monitored restraints may protect the suture line; comfort measures should avoid pressure or trauma to the repair.
rationales.B: Prone positioning can place pressure on the repair and is generally avoided.
rationales.C: A pacifier can traumatize the repair depending on the surgical plan and should not be used unless specifically approved.
rationales.D: Vigorous dry cleansing can disrupt the incision; follow the prescribed gentle cleaning regimen.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 7-year-old male admitted 2 weeks after untreated streptococcal pharyngitis with periorbital edema and dark smoky-brown urine.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Periorbital and facial puffiness worse in the morning, mild headache, bibasilar crackles.

questions.stem: A child with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis has periorbital edema, oliguria, and blood pressure above the age-specific 99th percentile. Which complication requires the closest immediate surveillance?

options.text: Hypertensive encephalopathy or pulmonary edema from fluid and sodium retention
Hypovolemic shock caused by urinary protein loss
Severe hypoglycemia caused by impaired renal glucose production
Spontaneous bleeding caused by platelet destruction

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Reduced filtration causes sodium and water retention, creating risk for severe hypertension, encephalopathy, and pulmonary edema.
rationales.B: Nephritic syndrome is characterized by fluid retention rather than massive protein loss and hypovolemia.
rationales.C: Hypoglycemia is not the characteristic acute complication.
rationales.D: Platelet destruction is not part of the typical pathophysiology.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 18-month-old toddler brought to the clinic with 24 hours of watery diarrhea and 3 episodes of vomiting from viral gastroenteritis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Alert, slightly dry oral mucosa, tears present when crying, capillary refill 2 seconds, 4% weight loss from baseline.
medications: Ondansetron 2 mg orally disintegrating tablet once
provider_orders: Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) 50 mL/kg over 4 hours

questions.stem: A toddler with gastroenteritis has mild dehydration and vomited once after drinking a large amount of fluid. Which instruction should the nurse give the parent?

options.text: Offer small, frequent amounts of oral rehydration solution and increase the volume gradually as tolerated
Give undiluted juice or sports drink in large amounts to replace electrolytes quickly
Withhold all fluids for 4 hours after any episode of vomiting
Use an antidiarrheal medication after each loose stool to reduce fluid loss

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Small frequent amounts of oral rehydration solution are often better tolerated and replace water and electrolytes in appropriate proportions.
rationales.B: Juice and sports drinks have inappropriate sugar and electrolyte concentrations and can worsen diarrhea.
rationales.C: Prolonged fluid withholding worsens dehydration; restart small amounts promptly after brief pauses if vomiting occurs.
rationales.D: Antidiarrheals are generally not recommended for young children with infectious diarrhea unless specifically prescribed.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 28-year-old male admitted to the inpatient behavioral health unit following a severe depressive episode with suicidal ideation.
clinical_scenario.assessment: After 3 days of appearing withdrawn and tearful, the client suddenly appears calm, cheerful, and gives his favorite wristwatch to another client.
medications: Sertraline 50 mg PO daily (started 3 days ago)

questions.stem: A hospitalized client with major depression who recently described a specific suicide plan suddenly appears calm and gives away valued belongings. What is the nurse's priority response?

options.text: Immediately reassess suicidal intent, plan, means, and access; maintain the prescribed observation level and notify the treatment team
Interpret the calm behavior as evidence that the antidepressant has taken full effect and reduce observation
Praise the generosity and encourage the client to complete the remaining personal arrangements
Avoid asking about suicide because direct questions may increase suicidal thoughts

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Sudden calmness and giving away possessions can signal preparation or a decision to attempt suicide; immediate reassessment and safety measures are required.
rationales.B: Antidepressants do not achieve full effect in a few days, and risk can remain high or increase as energy returns.
rationales.C: Reinforcing potentially preparatory behavior without assessment is unsafe.
rationales.D: Direct, nonjudgmental suicide assessment does not increase suicidal behavior and is essential.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 47-year-old male admitted 36 hours ago after a femur fracture; last drink of alcohol was 40 hours ago.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Agitated, diaphoretic, coarse hand tremors, reports seeing insects crawling on the walls; CIWA-Ar score is 22.
medications: Lorazepam 2 mg IV every 1 hour PRN CIWA-Ar > 15

questions.stem: A client with heavy daily alcohol use is 40 hours from the last drink and develops tremor, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and visual disturbances. Which medication class is the priority to prevent withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens?

options.text: Benzodiazepines titrated to withdrawal severity using the facility protocol
Antipsychotic monotherapy to suppress agitation and hallucinations
Disulfiram to create an aversive response to alcohol
Naltrexone to prevent alcohol craving during the acute withdrawal phase

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Benzodiazepines are first-line for moderate to severe alcohol withdrawal and reduce seizure and delirium risk.
rationales.B: Antipsychotics may be adjuncts for severe agitation but do not prevent withdrawal seizures and can lower seizure threshold.
rationales.C: Disulfiram is not used for acute withdrawal and requires abstinence.
rationales.D: Naltrexone is for relapse prevention, not acute withdrawal management.

questions.subtopic: Serotonin Syndrome vs. Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 33-year-old female taking fluoxetine 40 mg daily who was recently prescribed tramadol and linezolid.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Agitated, diaphoretic, shivering, hyperreflexia (4+ patellar reflexes), inducible ankle clonus, dilated pupils.

questions.stem: A client taking an SSRI recently added tramadol and linezolid. The client develops agitation, diaphoresis, inducible ankle clonus, and hyperreflexia. Which finding most strongly supports serotonin syndrome over neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

options.text: Clonus and hyperreflexia
Lead-pipe rigidity with markedly reduced reflexes
Fever and autonomic instability alone
Altered mental status without neuromuscular findings

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Clonus and hyperreflexia are characteristic neuromuscular findings of serotonin toxicity, especially with serotonergic drug combinations.
rationales.B: Lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia are more typical of NMS.
rationales.C: Fever and autonomic instability can occur in both syndromes and are less discriminating.
rationales.D: Mental-status changes occur in both and are not sufficient to distinguish them.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 26-year-old male admitted with an acute exacerbation of schizophrenia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Staring intently toward the corner of the dayroom, whispering, and covering his ears; states, 'The voices are telling me that the staff are poisoning my lunch.'

questions.stem: A client with schizophrenia says, 'The voices say the staff are putting poison in my food.' Which response is most therapeutic and supports safety assessment?

options.text: That sounds frightening. I do not hear the voices, but I want to understand what they are telling you and whether they are asking you to hurt yourself or anyone else.
The staff would never poison you, so you should ignore the voices and eat your meal.
Why do you keep believing things that are not real?
I hear them too, and I will make sure they stop talking to you.

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: The response acknowledges distress without validating the hallucination and assesses for command content and safety risk.
rationales.B: False reassurance and confrontation may undermine trust and do not assess risk.
rationales.C: Judgmental language can increase defensiveness and distress.
rationales.D: Claiming to hear the voices reinforces the hallucination and is not therapeutic.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: Medical-surgical nursing team consisting of an RN, an LPN/LVN, and an experienced unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) caring for four assigned clients.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Morning shift assignments are being delegated at 0715.

questions.stem: The RN is assigning tasks to an experienced UAP and an LPN on a medical-surgical unit. Which task is appropriate for the RN to delegate to the UAP?

options.text: Obtain routine vital signs and assist a stable client who is 2 days after uncomplicated surgery with ambulation
Complete the initial swallow screen for a client admitted with a possible stroke
Evaluate a new report of chest pain and determine whether it requires rapid response activation
Teach a client how to self-administer a new anticoagulant injection

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Routine, predictable tasks for a stable client can be delegated to trained UAP with clear instructions and follow-up.
rationales.B: Initial assessment and screening requiring clinical judgment remain with licensed staff according to policy.
rationales.C: Assessment and escalation decisions require RN judgment.
rationales.D: Initial teaching and evaluation of learning are nursing responsibilities.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: Registered nurse on an acute medical-surgical step-down unit receiving morning shift report on four assigned clients.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Four clients require immediate attention after shift handoff.

vital_signs.Summary: Client 1: SpO2 95%; Client 2: HR 88 bpm; Client 3: Stridor; Client 4: Temp 37.9 C

questions.stem: The RN receives report on four clients. Which client should be assessed first?

options.text: A client 4 hours after anterior cervical spine surgery who has new stridor and increasing neck swelling
A client with heart failure who is due for furosemide and has potassium of 4.0 mEq/L
A client 2 days after knee replacement requesting prescribed analgesia for pain rated 6/10
A client with cellulitis whose scheduled antibiotic infusion has just completed

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Stridor and neck swelling after anterior cervical surgery suggest an expanding hematoma and impending airway obstruction; immediate assessment and emergency response are required.
rationales.B: The medication is scheduled and the potassium is within typical range; this client is stable compared with an airway threat.
rationales.C: Pain requires treatment but is not the immediate threat described.
rationales.D: A completed infusion is routine and can be addressed after the airway emergency.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 68-year-old female admitted with profuse watery diarrhea and abdominal cramping after completing a 10-day course of clindamycin.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Mild lower abdominal tenderness, skin intact.
medications: Oral vancomycin 125 mg PO four times daily x 10 days

questions.stem: A client has confirmed Clostridioides difficile infection with frequent watery stools. Which infection-control actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use gown and gloves on room entry and dedicate equipment when possible
Wash hands with soap and water after care, especially when leaving the room
Use an EPA-registered sporicidal disinfectant for environmental cleaning
Rely on alcohol hand rub alone because it reliably kills C. difficile spores
Maintain contact precautions according to facility policy, including appropriate duration after diarrhea resolves

rationales.summary: The best answer is supported by the client's specific cues, immediate risks, and safe nursing priorities.
rationales.A: Contact precautions and dedicated equipment reduce spread of spores.
rationales.B: Soap and water mechanically remove spores; alcohol hand rub is not reliably sporicidal.
rationales.C: Environmental sporicidal products are needed to reduce contamination.
rationales.D: Alcohol alone does not reliably kill C. difficile spores.
rationales.E: Precaution duration follows facility and public-health guidance, often continuing after symptom resolution.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: Emergency department nurse performing START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) mass-casualty triage following a multi-vehicle highway collision.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Four victims arrive simultaneously and are evaluated using Respirations, Perfusion, and Mental Status (RPM).

vital_signs.Summary: Victim 1: RR 34, radial pulse present, follows commands; Victim 2: Apneic even after head-tilt/jaw-thrust; Victim 3: RR 18, capillary refill 1 sec, obeys commands, closed radius fracture; Victim 4: RR 20, capillary refill 2 sec, obeys commands, bilateral femur fractures unable to walk

provider_orders: Assign START triage color tags (Red/Immediate, Yellow/Delayed, Green/Minor, Black/Expectant)

questions.stem: Use START triage criteria to assign one tag to each victim. Apply the sequence: ambulatory status, respirations, perfusion, then ability to follow commands.

rows.text: Victim 1: RR 34 breaths/min, radial pulse present, obeys commands
Victim 2: Apneic even after airway repositioning maneuver
Victim 3: Walking wounded with a closed forearm fracture, RR 18, cap refill 1 sec, alert
Victim 4: Non-ambulatory with bilateral femur fractures, RR 20, cap refill 2 sec, alert

rationales.summary: START uses simple physiologic criteria to allocate resources rapidly. A respiratory rate above 30/min is red; apnea persisting after airway repositioning is black; ambulatory victims are green; nonambulatory victims with normal respirations, perfusion, and mental status are yellow.
rationales.V1: Red: respiratory rate is 34/min, exceeding the START threshold of 30/min.
rationales.V2: Black: the victim remains apneic after airway repositioning.
rationales.V3: Green: the victim can walk and has reassuring respiratory, perfusion, and mental-status findings.
rationales.V4: Yellow: the victim cannot walk but has RR below 30/min, capillary refill within 2 seconds, and follows commands.
